units.text: The skin works as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ: reviews describe four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells make and respond to hormones and signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the circulation. This is a mechanistic framework drawn from cell, tissue and animal work.

assertions.text: The skin functions as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ composed of four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells synthesize and respond to hormones and signal locally, through sensory nerves, and via the circulation.
assertions.quote: The skin neuro–immuno–endocrine system is composed of epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal immune–endocrine units, the activities of which are coordinated by sensory nerves.
assertions.note: Slominski et al. (2025) describe the skin neuro-immuno-endocrine system and its compartmentalization into epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal regulatory units coordinating local and systemic signalling.

assertions.text: The neuro-immuno-endocrine model of the skin is a mechanistic framework validated and supported experimentally across cell, tissue, and animal work.
assertions.quote: The original hypothesis that the skin is a neuroendocrine organ that secretes neuroendocrine and immune mediators to regulate local responses against environmental stress with systemic implications 17 , 45 has been validated and supported both experimentally and conceptually 2 , 3 , 16 , 36 , 46 – 49 .
assertions.note: The source notes that the hypothesis of the skin as a neuroendocrine organ has been validated experimentally and conceptually across diverse in vitro and in vivo models.

units.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally; this rests mainly on cell, tissue and biochemical studies.

assertions.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (such as CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (such as 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, and aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT, and estradiol locally.
assertions.quote: Most recently it has been established that skin cells contain the entire biochemical apparatus necessary for production of glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens either from precursors of systemic origin or, alternatively, through the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone and its subsequent transformation to biologically active steroids.
assertions.note: Slominski (2013) describes the complete biochemical apparatus in skin cells for de novo synthesis and precursor activation producing cortisol, DHT, and estradiol.

assertions.text: Evidence for cutaneous steroidogenesis rests mainly on cell, tissue, and biochemical studies.
assertions.note: While the cited reviews detail numerous in vitro, tissue, and biochemical assays, the provided text does not contain a summary statement characterizing the overall evidence base as resting mainly on these study types.

recheck.note: The provided texts discuss findings from in vitro, cell, and tissue models of cutaneous steroidogenesis, but do not state that the evidence rests mainly on these types of studies.

units.text: Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by making POMC products, secrete cortisol, and switch off their own CRH in response to glucocorticoid — an HPA-like loop running without systemic connections (human tissue, ex vivo).

assertions.text: Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by making POMC products and secreting cortisol.
assertions.quote: We show that microdissected, organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles respond to CRH stimulation by up-regulating proopiomelanocortin (POMC) transcription and immunoreactivity (IR) for ACTH and alpha-MSH, which must have been processed from POMC.
assertions.note: Organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles respond to CRH by up-regulating POMC transcription, processing it into ACTH and alpha-MSH, and secreting cortisol.

assertions.text: Hair follicles down-regulate their own CRH in response to glucocorticoids, operating an HPA-like feedback loop without systemic connections.
assertions.quote: Thus, even in the absence of endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections, normal human scalp hair follicles directly respond to CRH stimulation in a strikingly similar manner to what is seen in the classical HPA axis, including synthesis and secretion of cortisol and activation of prototypic neuroendocrine feedback loops.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that hydrocortisone down-regulates CRH expression and this HPA-like loop functions in the absence of systemic endocrine, neural, or vascular connections.

units.text: In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes causes spontaneous skin inflammation and worse experimental dermatitis: keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids set local immune tone (animal evidence, with a human association with inflammatory skin disease).

assertions.text: In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes causes spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.quote: In line with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency in human inflammatory skin disorders, genetic in vivo Cyp11b1 ablation and long-term GC deficiency in keratinocytes primed the murine skin immune system resulting in spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.note: The study demonstrated that keratinocyte-specific Cyp11b1 ablation leads to spontaneous skin inflammation in mice.

assertions.text: In mice, keratinocyte glucocorticoid deficiency exacerbates experimental dermatitis models.
assertions.quote: Deficient skin GC in experimental models for inflammatory skin disorders led to exacerbated contact hypersensitivity and psoriasiform skin inflammation accompanied by decreased regulatory T cells and the involvement of unconventional T cells.
assertions.note: Ablation of keratinocyte glucocorticoid synthesis worsened experimental contact hypersensitivity and psoriasiform skin inflammation.

assertions.text: Keratinocyte-synthesized glucocorticoids control skin immune homeostasis and set local immune tone.
assertions.quote: Keratinocytes control tissue homeostasis and skin inflammation via immunosuppressive glucocorticoids.
assertions.note: The paper demonstrates that keratinocyte-derived glucocorticoids regulate skin tissue homeostasis and immune microenvironment.

assertions.text: Steroidogenic enzyme deficiency and dysregulated skin glucocorticoid synthesis are associated with human inflammatory skin disorders.
assertions.quote: These results confirm previous studies indicating that epidermal steroidogenesis is dysregulated in prevalent inflammatory skin disorders, such as AD and psoriasis ( 17 , 18 ).
assertions.note: Epidermal steroidogenesis enzymes like CYP11B1 were found to be decreased in human atopic dermatitis and psoriatic skin lesions.

units.text: The skin also runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops; the thyroid-like evidence comes mainly from mouse models and the follicle GH/IGF-1 loop from human follicles ex vivo.

assertions.text: The skin operates a shortened thyroid-like pathway involving TRH, TSH receptors, and deiodinase-generated T3, with mechanistic evidence derived largely from mouse models.
assertions.quote: Surprisingly, the expression of fully functional proteins typical of the HPT axis and in particular of the TSH and TRH receptors has been found in human skin and in HFs [ 27 ]. Receptors for TSH and TRH in the skin induce the expression of skin-specific genes [ 28 ] and thus regulate epidermal physiology, adding a mechanistic explanation of the correlation between the altered TH status and the most common dermatology diseases [ 29 ].
assertions.note: Mancino et al. describe the expression of functional HPT-axis proteins (TSH and TRH receptors), local deiodinase generation of T3, and the extensive use of mouse models to elucidate these mechanisms.

assertions.text: The hair follicle operates a somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loop demonstrated in human follicles ex vivo.
assertions.note: The cited sources covering the hair follicle somatotropic axis (Horesh et al., 2023 and Hannah-Shmouni, 2026) are unavailable.

units.text: The skin supplies a whole-body hormone system: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin, and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation to be hydroxylated to 25(OH)D and then calcitriol (skin-to-body signalling).

assertions.text: UVB radiation converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into previtamin D3 in human skin.
assertions.quote: D3 (cholecalciferol) is produced from 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) through a two-step process in which the B ring is broken by UV light (spectrum 280–320 UVB) radiation from the sun, forming pre-D3 that isomerizes to D3 in a thermo-sensitive but noncatalytic process.
assertions.note: Bikle (2014) confirms that 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin is converted by solar UVB into previtamin D3.

assertions.text: Vitamin D3 is transported into the bloodstream and hydroxylated sequentially to 25(OH)D and calcitriol (1,25(OH)2D).
assertions.quote: Vitamin D is metabolized first to 25 hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD), then to the hormonal form 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D).
assertions.note: Holick et al. (1980) and Bikle (2014) confirm the transport of vitamin D3 into the circulation and its sequential hydroxylation to 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D.

units.text: Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, especially in older people — a second skin-to-body route, supported mainly by biochemical data.

assertions.text: Reviews describe a cutaneous contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, particularly in older individuals.
assertions.quote: Human skin produces, activates or inactivates metabolically numerous hormones which are probably important for skin functions but also for functions of the entire human organism, such as sex hormones, especially in aged individuals, insulin-like growth factor and -binding proteins, neuropeptides, prolactin, catecholamines, retinoids, steroids, vitamin D and eicosanoids.
assertions.note: The review states that human skin produces hormones released into circulation, including sex hormones especially in aged individuals.

assertions.text: Evidence for cutaneous production and systemic contribution of active steroids is established through biochemical apparatus and steroidogenic pathway data.
assertions.quote: Most recently it has been established that skin cells contain the entire biochemical apparatus necessary for production of glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens either from precursors of systemic origin or, alternatively, through the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone and its subsequent transformation to biologically active steroids.
assertions.note: The review notes that skin cells contain the entire biochemical apparatus for producing glucocorticoids, androgens, and estrogens.

units.text: Systemic hormones act on skin (body-to-skin): cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising; hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse skin and myxoedema. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.

assertions.text: Cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising.
assertions.note: The provided text on thyroid hormone action does not discuss cortisol excess causing striae or bruising, and the cited guide is unavailable.

assertions.text: Hypothyroidism causes dry, coarse skin and myxoedema.
assertions.quote: Generalized myxedema is still the classic cutaneous sign of hypothyroidism. It is caused by deposition of dermal acid mucopolysaccharides, notably hyaluronic acid.
assertions.note: The source confirms that hypothyroidism causes coarsened, dry skin and generalized myxedema.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.
assertions.note: The cited book is unavailable in the provided sources.

units.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science 2026) analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them, and mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues, mapping putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.
assertions.quote: Drawing inspiration from the Human Cell Atlas, we analyzed the expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes in a transcriptomic dataset comprising 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues. Using hormone2cell, we mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types, defining tissue-specific and cross-tissue endocrine signatures.
assertions.note: The abstract explicitly confirms analyzing 379 hormone and receptor genes across 14 million single cells and nuclei in 47 human tissues to map putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.

assertions.text: The 47 human tissues analysed in the Hormone Cell Atlas included skin.
assertions.note: The provided source texts mention 47 human tissues in total but do not specify whether skin was among them.

units.text: The atlas's authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating, not functional hormones and receptors, and leave validation to in vitro and in vivo work; more generally, transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels. A transcriptomic map therefore shows capacity, not secretion or effect.

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating rather than functional hormones and receptors, leaving validation to in vitro and in vivo work.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors. The user takes responsibility for validation using appropriate methods (e.g. in vitro, in vivo) and for describing appropriately their use of transcriptome-based scores and predictions.
assertions.note: The portal documentation states that predictions are putative and hypothesis-generating rather than functional hormones and receptors, with validation left to methods such as in vitro and in vivo testing.

assertions.text: Transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels.
assertions.quote: We conclude that transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios and to thus explain genotype-phenotype relationships and that high-quality data quantifying different levels of gene expression are indispensable for the complete understanding of biological processes.
assertions.note: Liu et al. conclude that transcript levels alone are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios.

assertions.text: A transcriptomic map shows capacity, not secretion or effect.
assertions.note: While the sources note transcriptomic predictions are putative, this specific characterization of transcriptomic maps is not stated in the provided text.

assertions.text: The skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks based on transcriptomic prediction from the hormone cell atlas.
assertions.note: The provided abstract does not mention skin or its role as an endocrine signalling network, and the pocket guide source is unavailable.

assertions.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin carries, and local steroid-metabolising enzymes modify potency so cutaneous response does not necessarily mirror dose.

assertions.note: The source states that transcriptomic predictions of hormone receptors are putative and hypothesis-generating requiring validation (such as in vitro or in vivo), but does not specify human clinical trials.

units.text: Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested yet metabolically active; the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, growth factors) was characterised in cultured human cells after DNA damage.

assertions.text: Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested.
assertions.quote: Cellular senescence is an irreversible growth arrest that occurs as a result of different damaging stimuli, including DNA damage, telomere shortening and dysfunction or oncogenic stress.
assertions.note: The sources state that cellular senescence entails an irreversible/essentially permanent growth arrest.

assertions.text: Senescent cells are metabolically active.
assertions.note: The provided text does not explicitly mention that senescent cells remain metabolically active.

recheck.note: The provided source texts describe senescent cells as actively secreting diverse factors (SASP) rather than being passive, but do not specifically state that they are metabolically active.

assertions.text: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype (including IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, and growth factors) was characterised in cultured human cells after DNA damage.
assertions.quote: For instance, senescent cells modulate their environment by secreting inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and growth factors, collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) ( Acosta et al., 2008 ; Coppé et al., 2008b ; Kuilman et al., 2008 ; Rodier et al., 2009 ) or senescence-messaging secretome (SMS) ( Kuilman and Peeper, 2009 ).
assertions.note: The paper characterizes SASP components including IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, and growth factors following genotoxic/DNA damage in human cells in culture.

units.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both epidermis and dermis; no single universal marker identifies senescent cells, so counts depend on the marker used.

assertions.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both epidermis and dermis.
assertions.quote: The number of p16INK4A positive cells was found to be increased in both epidermis and dermis, compartments with strictly different proliferative activities.
assertions.note: Ressler et al. found an age-dependent increase in p16INK4a-positive cells in both epidermal and dermal skin compartments.

assertions.text: No single universal marker identifies senescent cells, so counts depend on the marker used.
assertions.quote: However, a significant hurdle in the aging field has been the identification of a universal biomarker that facilitates the unequivocal detection and quantification of senescent cell types in vitro and in vivo .
assertions.note: Wang and Dreesen note that identifying a universal biomarker for senescent cells remains an unresolved hurdle in the field.

units.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age independent of chronological age; people in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest. This is an association, not evidence of cause.

assertions.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles, and higher perceived age independent of chronological age.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that in 178 Leiden Longevity Study participants, p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin associated with age-associated elastic fibre morphology, facial wrinkles, and perceived age adjusted for chronological age.

assertions.text: Participants in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile.
assertions.quote: Participants in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16INK4a counts looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile, independently of chronological age and elastic fiber morphology.
assertions.note: The abstract directly states that participants in the lowest tertile looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile.

units.text: Skin collagen falls with age; aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1, fragmented collagen and fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that make less procollagen, and culture work shows fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.

assertions.text: Skin collagen falls with age.
assertions.quote: Skin collagen decreased with age and was less in the females at all ages.
assertions.note: The abstract explicitly states that skin collagen decreases with age.

assertions.text: Aged human dermis shows increased fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen.
assertions.quote: We report here that dermal fibroblasts express increased levels of collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinases-1 (MMP-1) in aged (>80 years old) compared with young (21 to 30 years old) human skin in vivo.
assertions.note: Aged human skin exhibits elevated MMP-1 expression by dermal fibroblasts alongside collagen fibril fragmentation.

assertions.text: Aged human dermis shows fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that produce less procollagen.
assertions.quote: The reduction in collagen synthesis due to fibroblast aging was demonstrated by a lower in vitro production of type I procollagen by dermal fibroblasts isolated from skin of young (18 to 29 years) versus old (80+ years) individuals (82 +/- 16 versus 56 +/- 8 ng/ml; P < 0.05).
assertions.note: Old skin exhibits reduced mechanical stimulation on fibroblasts and lower procollagen synthesis compared to young skin.

assertions.text: Culture work demonstrates that collagen fragmentation feeds back to elevate MMP-1.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, fibroblasts cultured in fragmented collagen lattices express elevated levels of MMP-1, AP-1, and alpha2beta1 integrin.
assertions.note: Fibroblasts cultured in fragmented collagen express elevated MMP-1 in a positive feedback loop.

assertions.text: That senescent cells drive collagen loss and fragmentation in living skin is plausible but not shown.
assertions.note: The provided abstracts do not discuss whether senescent cells drive this process in living skin.

units.text: Causal evidence that senescent cells drive ageing comes from mice: clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan and senolytics improved function and survival in old mice; skin was not an endpoint.

assertions.text: In mice, clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan.
assertions.quote: Here we show that compared to vehicle alone, AP20187 treatment extended median lifespan in both male and female mice of two distinct genetic backgrounds.
assertions.note: Clearing p16-positive cells with AP20187 extended median lifespan in both male and female mice across two genetic backgrounds.

assertions.text: Senolytics improved physical function and survival in old mice.
assertions.quote: Moreover, intermittent oral administration of senolytics to both senescent cell-transplanted younger and naturally-aged mice alleviated physical dysfunction and increased post-treatment survival by 36% while reducing mortality hazard to 65%.
assertions.note: Intermittent senolytic treatment alleviated physical dysfunction and increased post-treatment survival in naturally aged mice.

assertions.text: Skin was not an endpoint in these mouse studies.
assertions.quote: iWAT cell diameter, adipose depot weight, skin thickness, and skeletal muscle diameter measurements were as described 4.
assertions.note: Skin thickness, cutaneous wound healing, and skin fibrosis were explicitly evaluated as endpoints.

units.text: Human senotherapy data are small pilots with tissue-marker endpoints — an open-label senolytic pilot in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16/p21-positive cells; an exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 lost) reduced skin p16 — and no randomized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (checked 24 September 2026). The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.

assertions.text: An open-label senolytic pilot study in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16- and p21-positive cells.
assertions.quote: Skin epidermal p16 INK4A+ and p21 CIP1+ cells were reduced, as were circulating SASP factors, including IL-1α, IL-6, and MMPs-9 and −12.
assertions.note: The pilot trial in 9 patients with diabetic kidney disease confirmed a reduction in epidermal p16INK4A+ and p21CIP1+ cells.

assertions.text: An exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 lost to follow-up/discontinued) reduced skin p16 levels.
assertions.quote: Thirty-six participants were enrolled in the study, and nineteen discontinued or were lost to follow-up. A significant ( P = 0.008) reduction in p16 INK4A protein levels and an increase in collagen VII protein levels ( P = 0.0077) were observed among participants at the end of the study.
assertions.note: The prospective randomized trial with 36 enrolled and 19 dropouts/losses to follow-up reported a significant reduction in skin p16INK4A protein levels.

assertions.text: No randomized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov as of 24 September 2026.
assertions.note: The specific literature search details and cutoff date are not contained in the provided source texts.

assertions.text: The clinical guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.
assertions.note: The cited pocket guide is unavailable in the provided sources.

units.text: Interventions on the ageing matrix with human trials: daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT (B); topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials and the guide rates topical retinoids first-line GRADE A; topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT (C), and within a week lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis in aged human skin.

assertions.text: Daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: Hughes et al. reported a 24% reduction in skin aging in a community-based randomized trial of 903 adults.

assertions.text: Topical tretinoin consistently improves photoageing across randomized trials.
assertions.quote: With regard to efficacy, all studies consistently reported that topical tretinoin was efficacious in improving clinical appearance of photoaging in terms of wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines as early as 1 month and lasted after 24 months.
assertions.note: A systematic review of 7 RCTs confirmed consistent efficacy across trials.

assertions.text: A clinical guide rates topical retinoids as first-line GRADE A for photoageing.
assertions.note: The cited guideline source text is unavailable in the repository.

assertions.text: Topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT.
assertions.quote: Topical retinol improves fine wrinkles associated with natural aging.
assertions.note: A randomized trial in 36 elderly participants (mean age 87) found significant improvement in fine wrinkling.

assertions.text: Topical retinol lowered MMP levels and raised collagen synthesis within a week in aged human skin.
assertions.quote: In a separate group of 53 individuals (80+ y of age), topical application of 1% vitamin A for 7 d increased fibroblast growth and collagen synthesis, and concomitantly reduced the levels of matrix-degrading matrix metalloproteinases.
assertions.note: Application of 1% vitamin A for 7 days lowered matrix metalloproteinases and increased collagen synthesis in elderly subjects.

units.text: The skin expresses the elements of a local HPA-like axis (CRH, POMC, ACTH) and regenerates active cortisol from cortisone through 11β-HSD1 in keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts; 11β-HSD1 activity is higher in aged and photo-exposed human skin, local glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of circulating levels, and 11β-HSD1 knockout mice are protected from age-induced dermal atrophy.

assertions.text: The skin expresses the elements of a local HPA-like axis, including CRH, POMC, and ACTH.
assertions.quote: In fact, all of the elements controlling the activity of the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis are expressed in the skin including CRH, urocortin, and POMC, with its products ACTH, alpha-MSH, and beta-endorphin.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that the elements of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, including CRH, POMC, and ACTH, are expressed locally in skin.

assertions.text: 11β-HSD1 is expressed in keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts where it regenerates active cortisol from cortisone.
assertions.quote: 11β-HSD1 (which activates cortisol), but not 11β-HSD2 (which inactivates cortisol), was expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts in human skin and also in outer hair follicle root sheath cells in murine skin.
assertions.note: 11β-HSD1, which activates cortisol, is expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts in human skin.

assertions.text: Local tissue glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of systemic circulating levels.
assertions.quote: Within target tissues, GC availability is regulated at a prereceptor level, independently of systemic levels, by isozymes of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) that interconvert active cortisol and inactive cortisone.
assertions.note: The cited study states that glucocorticoid availability is regulated at the prereceptor level within target tissues independently of systemic levels.

assertions.text: 11β-HSD1 activity is elevated in aged and photo-exposed human skin.
assertions.quote: 11β-HSD1 activity was elevated in aged human and mouse skin and in PE compared with donor-matched photo-protected human biopsies.
assertions.note: The study confirms 11β-HSD1 activity is elevated in aged human skin and in photo-exposed relative to photo-protected biopsies.

assertions.text: 11β-HSD1 knockout mice are protected from age-induced dermal atrophy.
assertions.quote: Age-induced dermal atrophy with deranged collagen structural organization was prevented in 11β-HSD1 KO mice, which also exhibited increased collagen density.
assertions.note: The cited study confirms age-induced dermal atrophy was prevented in 11β-HSD1 knockout mice.

units.text: The only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes is a 28-person pilot in type 2 diabetes: it missed its primary outcome (skin 11β-HSD1 activity), showed an exploratory reduction in wound size, and modestly impaired barrier function. No registered trial tests an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for skin ageing, and the compound tested has no FDA approval (ClinicalTrials.gov and Drugs@FDA checked 24 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: A 28-person pilot RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition in type 2 diabetes missed its primary outcome of skin 11β-HSD1 activity.
assertions.quote: In this pilot study, data on our primary outcome measure failed to show 11β-HSD1 inhibition in the skin.
assertions.note: The pilot trial failed to demonstrate inhibition of skin 11β-HSD1 activity as its primary endpoint.

assertions.text: The trial showed an exploratory reduction in wound size and modestly impaired barrier function.
assertions.quote: Wound diameter was 34% (7–63%) smaller with AZD4017 at day 2, and 48% (12–85%) smaller after repeat wounding at day 30. AZD4017 improved epidermal integrity but modestly impaired barrier function.
assertions.note: Wound diameter was reduced at day 2 and day 30, while epidermal barrier function was modestly impaired.

assertions.text: No registered trial tests an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for skin ageing, and the tested compound has no FDA approval.
assertions.note: The provided text does not contain registry-wide searches for skin ageing trials or FDA regulatory approval status.

units.text: Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm; facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory.

assertions.text: Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy, and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm.
assertions.note: The abstract mentions testing patients with features of high discriminatory value but does not list the specific discriminating features.

assertions.text: Facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin, and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory for Cushing's syndrome.
assertions.note: These specific features and their prevalence or discriminatory value are not detailed in the provided abstract.

units.text: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon (2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies); the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, and the guideline recommends a drug history (oral, inhaled, topical, injected — including skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections) before any biochemical testing.

assertions.text: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome has an incidence of 2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies.
assertions.note: The provided abstract does not mention incidence rates or European population studies.

assertions.text: The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic.
assertions.note: The provided abstract does not state that iatrogenic causes are the most common.

assertions.text: The guideline recommends taking a drug history covering all glucocorticoid routes (oral, inhaled, topical, injected, herbal tonics) to exclude exogenous use before any biochemical testing.
assertions.quote: After excluding exogenous glucocorticoid use, we recommend testing for Cushing's syndrome in patients with multiple and progressive features compatible with the syndrome, particularly those with a high discriminatory value, and patients with adrenal incidentaloma.
assertions.note: The abstract recommends excluding exogenous glucocorticoid use before testing, but does not detail the specific administration routes or products.

units.text: The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly the discriminating ones) or features unusual for age, recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol, and sends abnormal results to an endocrinologist. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide adds that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated and reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.

assertions.text: The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly the discriminating ones) or features unusual for age.
assertions.quote: After excluding exogenous glucocorticoid use, we recommend testing for Cushing's syndrome in patients with multiple and progressive features compatible with the syndrome, particularly those with a high discriminatory value, and patients with adrenal incidentaloma.
assertions.note: The abstract supports testing patients with multiple and progressive features with high discriminatory value, but does not mention features unusual for age.

assertions.text: The guideline recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol.
assertions.note: The abstract does not explicitly state recommendations against widespread testing or against random serum cortisol.

assertions.text: The guideline recommends sending abnormal results to an endocrinologist.
assertions.quote: We recommend that patients with an abnormal result see an endocrinologist and undergo a second test, either one of the above or, in some cases, a serum midnight cortisol or dexamethasone-CRH test.
assertions.note: The guideline abstract recommends that patients with an abnormal initial test result see an endocrinologist.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide states that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated and reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.
assertions.note: The cited source text is unavailable.

units.text: Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ and GPR30 in aged and photoaged sites; two weeks of topical estradiol raised procollagen I/III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

assertions.text: Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ, and GPR30 in aged and photoaged sites.
assertions.quote: Surprisingly, no significant changes in production were observed in women or men after 2-week estradiol treatment of photoaged forearm or face skin, despite similar expression of estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30) in aged and photoaged skin.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms similar expression of ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30 in aged and photoaged skin.

assertions.text: Topical estradiol raised procollagen I and III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women.
assertions.quote: Topical estradiol increased procollagen I and III messenger RNA and collagen I protein levels in sun-protected aged hip skin in postmenopausal women and, to a lesser extent, in age-matched men.
assertions.note: Topical estradiol increased procollagen I and III mRNA in sun-protected aged hip skin in postmenopausal women.

assertions.text: Two weeks of topical estradiol did not increase collagen production in photoaged forearm or facial skin.
assertions.quote: Two-week topical estradiol treatment stimulates collagen production in sun-protected hip skin, but not in photoaged forearm or face skin, in postmenopausal women and aged-matched men.
assertions.note: No significant changes were observed after 2 weeks of estradiol treatment on photoaged forearm or face skin.

units.text: In small observational biopsy studies, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass, tracking years since menopause more than chronological age. The 'up to 30% in the first five years' figure quoted by reviews and by the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide is not stated in the primary abstracts it traces to; the lesson reports it as a review figure.

assertions.text: In postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass, tracking years since menopause more than chronological age.
assertions.note: Brincat et al. (1987) confirm a 1–2% annual postmenopausal decline in skin collagen, skin thickness, and bone mass correlated with years since menopause.

assertions.text: Literature reviews quote a decline in skin collagen of up to 30% in the first five years after menopause.
assertions.note: Thornton (2013) notes that type I and III skin collagen is thought to decrease by as much as 30% in the first five years after menopause.

units.text: Small RCTs of systemic hormone therapy increased skin thickness (n=60, 12 months) and skin collagen (n=41, 6 months) at non-facial sites; a 2023 meta-analysis pooling small, heterogeneous studies (some non-randomized) reports higher elasticity, thickness and collagen, and its authors do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.

assertions.text: A small randomized controlled trial (n=60, 12 months) found that systemic hormone therapy increased skin thickness at a non-facial site.
assertions.quote: Sixty postmenopausal women were randomly allocated to receive conjugated estrogens or placebo treatment for 12 months.
assertions.note: The cited trial abstract confirms 60 postmenopausal women received conjugated estrogens or placebo for 12 months and showed increased skin thickness at the right great trochanter.

assertions.text: A small randomized controlled trial (n=41, 6 months) found that systemic hormone therapy increased skin collagen at a non-facial site.
assertions.quote: Forty-one postmenopausal women were randomly allocated to receive either hormonal replacement (valerate estradiol--2 mg/day for 21 days and cyproterone acetate--1 mg/day for 10 days) or placebo, both in a cyclic scheme for 6 months.
assertions.note: The cited trial abstract confirms 41 postmenopausal women received HRT or placebo for 6 months and showed increased skin collagen content in the left upper arm.

assertions.text: A 2023 meta-analysis pooling small, heterogeneous studies (including non-randomized designs) reports higher skin elasticity, thickness, and collagen.
assertions.quote: Based on our systematic review and meta-analysis results, we can conclude that MHT increases elasticity and collagen content in the skin, thereby reducing the severity of wrinkles increasing skin thickness and firmness.
assertions.note: The 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled randomized and non-randomized studies and found statistically significant improvements in skin elasticity, thickness, and collagen content.

assertions.text: The authors of the 2023 meta-analysis do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.
assertions.quote: While not claiming that MHT can or should ever be considered as an independent treatment for skin ageing, we still believe that our results are interesting as they indicate a beneficial effect of MHT on the skin, despite studies showing a negative effect of MHT on other organs.
assertions.note: The authors explicitly state they do not claim MHT should be considered an independent treatment for skin ageing.

units.text: The largest RCT of hormone therapy on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks, low-dose) found no significant difference from placebo in wrinkling or sagging, and a 4-year randomized study in recently menopausal women (KEEPS) found no difference in wrinkle or rigidity scores. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the NAMS 2022 statement rates its skin key point Level II (limited or inconsistent); the course grades the structural effects C and states that a visible wrinkle benefit has not been shown in the largest trials.

assertions.text: The largest RCT of hormone therapy on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks, low-dose) found no significant difference from placebo in wrinkling or sagging.
assertions.quote: Four hundred eighty-five subjects were enrolled in this 48-week randomized, double-blind study. Subjects were randomized to one of three study arms: placebo group (165 subjects), 1 mg NA/5 microg EE group (162 subjects), or a 1 mg NA/10 microg EE group (158 subjects).
assertions.note: Phillips et al. found no statistically significant difference between low-dose NA/EE and placebo for wrinkling or sagging in 485 women over 48 weeks.

assertions.text: A 4-year randomized study in recently menopausal women (KEEPS) found no difference in wrinkle or rigidity scores.
assertions.quote: Neither total wrinkle score nor total rigidity score was significantly different at baseline or over the 4-year follow-up among patients randomized to CEE, E 2 , or placebo.
assertions.note: The KEEPS ancillary skin study found neither total wrinkle score nor total rigidity score differed over 4 years between hormone therapy and placebo.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B.
assertions.note: The cited source is unavailable.

assertions.text: The NAMS 2022 statement rates its skin key point Level II (limited or inconsistent).
assertions.note: The abstract of the NAMS 2022 position statement does not mention skin ratings or Level II evidence.

units.text: Topical estrogen: a 24-week RCT (n=54) of a conjugated-estrogen cream improved facial skin thickness and fine wrinkles versus placebo cream, and a small randomized study found topical estrogen accelerated acute wound healing in healthy older adults. In the US an OTC product promoted as a hormone cream is regarded as an unapproved new drug (21 CFR 310.530), and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises against off-label estrogen for wrinkles (GRADE C).

assertions.text: A 24-week RCT (n=54) of a conjugated-estrogen cream improved facial skin thickness and fine wrinkles versus placebo cream.
assertions.quote: In conclusion, Premarin cream produced better results than the placebo cream; the difference was statistically significant for skin thickness and fine wrinkles.
assertions.note: The study abstract confirms a 24-week randomized study of 54 women showing significant improvements in skin thickness and fine wrinkles with Premarin cream compared to placebo.

assertions.text: A small randomized study found topical estrogen accelerated acute wound healing in healthy older adults.
assertions.quote: These data demonstrate that delays in wound healing in the elderly can be significantly diminished by topical estrogen in both male and female subjects.
assertions.note: The study found that topical estrogen accelerated cutaneous wound healing and diminished delays in wound healing in healthy elderly men and women.

assertions.text: In the US an OTC product promoted as a hormone cream is regarded as an unapproved new drug under 21 CFR 310.530.
assertions.note: The provided source text is a website access/CAPTCHA block page and does not contain the regulatory text.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises against off-label estrogen for wrinkles (GRADE C).
assertions.note: The cited guide is unavailable.

units.text: In the US (FDA request of 10 Nov 2025; first approved labels 12 Feb 2026), approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal/genitourinary symptoms and, for some products, prevention of bone loss; the labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and probable-dementia statements from the boxed warning and did not add skin as an indication.

assertions.text: In the US, approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal/genitourinary symptoms, and, for some products, prevention of bone loss.
assertions.quote: FDA has approved numerous MHTs to treat moderate/severe hot flashes, VVA, and for some, prevention of bone thinning.
assertions.note: The FDA document confirms approved uses include moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal atrophy/GSM, and prevention of bone thinning/osteoporosis for some products.

assertions.text: The FDA labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer, and probable-dementia statements from the boxed warning.
assertions.quote: Specifically, risk statements related to cardiovascular disease, breast cancer and probable dementia were removed from the “boxed warning,” the agency’s most prominent safety-related warning.
assertions.note: The FDA announcement states risk statements for cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and probable dementia were removed from the boxed warning.

assertions.text: The FDA labeling changes did not add skin as an indication.
assertions.note: The provided FDA sources do not mention skin or skin-related indications.

units.text: The NAMS 2022 position statement finds the benefit–risk ratio favourable for bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss in women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause without contraindications, and finds insufficient evidence and safety concerns for compounded bioidentical hormone therapy (patient preference alone should not justify it); WHI findings do not support MHT for chronic disease prevention. Skin benefit is secondary and never on its own an indication (Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide).

assertions.text: The NAMS 2022 position statement finds the benefit–risk ratio favourable for bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss in women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset without contraindications.
assertions.quote: For women aged younger than 60 years or who are within 10 years of menopause onset and have no contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favorable for treatment of bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss.
assertions.note: The position statement abstract explicitly states the benefit-risk ratio is favorable for these indications in this population.

assertions.text: The NAMS 2022 position statement finds insufficient evidence and safety concerns for compounded bioidentical hormone therapy, stating patient preference alone should not justify it.
assertions.note: The provided abstract of the NAMS 2022 position statement does not mention compounded bioidentical hormone therapy.

assertions.text: WHI trial findings do not support menopausal hormone therapy for chronic disease prevention.
assertions.quote: While appropriate for symptom management in some women, its use for chronic disease prevention is not supported by the WHI randomized trials.
assertions.note: The WHI study conclusion explicitly notes that hormone therapy for chronic disease prevention is not supported.

assertions.text: Skin benefit is secondary and never on its own an indication for hormone therapy according to the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide.
assertions.note: The cited source is unavailable in the provided text.

units.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen is effective for moderate-to-severe genitourinary syndrome of menopause without an added progestogen — the one setting where estrogen is given for the tissue itself.

assertions.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen is effective for moderate-to-severe genitourinary syndrome of menopause without an added progestogen.
assertions.quote: Low-dose vaginal estrogens, vaginal DHEA, systemic estrogen therapy, and ospemifene are effective treatments for moderate to severe GSM. When low-dose vaginal estrogen or DHEA or ospemifene is administered, a progestogen is not indicated; however, endometrial safety has not been studied in clinical trials beyond 1 year.
assertions.note: The 2020 NAMS position statement confirms low-dose vaginal estrogens are effective for moderate-to-severe GSM and that a progestogen is not indicated.

assertions.text: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause is the one setting where estrogen is given for the tissue itself.
assertions.note: The provided abstracts do not state that GSM is the only clinical setting where estrogen is prescribed for local tissue effects.

units.text: Skin-directed care with stronger evidence: daily broad-spectrum sunscreen reduced measured skin ageing over 4.5 years in a 903-person independent RCT, and in the US one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for mitigating fine facial wrinkles (its label states it does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging).

assertions.text: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen reduced measured skin ageing over 4.5 years in a 903-person RCT.
assertions.quote: The daily sunscreen group showed no detectable increase in skin aging after 4.5 years. Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: A 903-adult RCT found 24% less skin aging progression over 4.5 years in the daily sunscreen group compared to discretionary use.

assertions.text: In the US, a tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunctive agent for mitigating fine facial wrinkles.
assertions.quote: RENOVA (tretinoin cream) 0.02% is indicated as an adjunctive agent (see second bullet point below) for use in the mitigation (palliation) of fine facial wrinkles in patients who use comprehensive skin care and sunlight avoidance programs.
assertions.note: The FDA label indicates RENOVA (tretinoin cream) as an adjunctive agent for the mitigation of fine facial wrinkles.

assertions.text: The tretinoin cream label states that it does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging.
assertions.quote: RENOVA (tretinoin cream) 0.02% DOES NOT ELIMINATE WRINKLES, REPAIR SUN-DAMAGED SKIN, REVERSE PHOTOAGING, or RESTORE MORE YOUTHFUL or YOUNGER SKIN.
assertions.note: The product label explicitly states it does not eliminate wrinkles, repair sun-damaged skin, or reverse photoaging.

units.text: In a consecutive NIH series of 32 people with MEN1, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas (identical to those of tuberous sclerosis) and 72% collagenomas; angiofibromas outside tuberous sclerosis warrant biochemical testing for MEN1.

assertions.text: In a consecutive NIH series of 32 patients with MEN1, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas (identical to those of tuberous sclerosis) and 72% had collagenomas.
assertions.quote: Multiple facial angiofibromas were observed in 28 (88%) of the patients with MEN1, with 16 patients (50%) having 5 or more. Angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those in individuals with tuberous sclerosis. Collagenomas were observed in 23 patients (72%).
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that in a consecutive sample of 32 patients with MEN1 examined at the NIH, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas (clinically and histologically identical to tuberous sclerosis) and 72% had collagenomas.

assertions.text: Finding angiofibromas in individuals without tuberous sclerosis warrants biochemical testing for MEN1.
assertions.quote: The observation of angiofibromas in individuals without tuberous sclerosis necessitates further biochemical testing for MEN1.
assertions.note: The study conclusions explicitly state that finding angiofibromas in individuals without tuberous sclerosis necessitates biochemical testing for MEN1.

units.text: Carney complex (over 70% carry inactivating PRKAR1A variants) presents with lentigines typically on the face, lips and mucosa (canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome), blue naevi and cutaneous myxomas (eyelid, ear, nipple); cardiac myxomas occur in 20–40% and cause more than half of disease mortality, which is why early detection and echocardiographic screening matter.

assertions.text: Over 70% of patients with Carney complex carry inactivating PRKAR1A variants.
assertions.quote: More than 70% of the patients diagnosed with CNC carry mutations on the PRKAR1A gene (CNC1 locus) and this percentage increases to 80% for those with Cushing’s syndrome due to primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD) .
assertions.note: Correa et al. confirm that more than 70% of CNC patients carry inactivating mutations in PRKAR1A.

assertions.text: Carney complex presents with lentigines typically distributed on the face, lips, and mucosa, blue naevi, and cutaneous myxomas (eyelid, ear, nipple).
assertions.quote: Cutaneous myxomas (Figure 1D–F) are found in 30–55% of CNC patients and usually appear in the eyelid, external ear canal, breast nipples, and the genitalia .
assertions.note: Correa et al. report this characteristic distribution of lentigines, blue nevi, and cutaneous myxomas.

assertions.text: Canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.
assertions.quote: inner or outer canthal pigmentation such as the one shown here is only seen in CNC and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome making it diagnostic for these two conditions.
assertions.note: Correa et al. state that canthal pigmentation is seen only in CNC and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

assertions.text: Cardiac myxomas occur in 20–40% of Carney complex patients and cause more than half of disease mortality.
assertions.quote: The most common noncutaneous lesions found in CNC are cardiac myxomas (in 20–40% of the patients)  which can appear early in infancy  but the median age at detection is at 20 years .
assertions.note: Correa et al. report that cardiac myxomas occur in 20–40% of CNC patients and account for more than 50% of the disease mortality.

units.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide's first-pass hair-loss workup: patterned thinning → androgenetic alopecia (topical minoxidil; finasteride in men; treat coexisting iron or thyroid problems); diffuse shedding after a trigger → telogen effluvium (remove the trigger, reassure, recheck ferritin and TSH); patchy smooth loss (± nail pitting) → alopecia areata (dermatology referral; screen thyroid and autoimmune disease); signs of androgen excess → hyperandrogenism work-up; always ferritin and TSH, androgens if virilising, biopsy a scarring pattern; refer severe or rapidly progressive alopecia areata promptly.

units.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis of good- or fair-quality RCTs found topical minoxidil (in men and in women) and oral finasteride (in men) superior to placebo for androgenetic alopecia.

units.text: Skin cells produce POMC and its products ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin and carry their receptors. Of the five melanocortin receptors, MC1R mediates pigmentation of skin and hair, MC2R adrenal steroidogenesis, MC3R and MC4R central control of food intake, and MC5R sebogenesis; true receptor distribution is probably wider than this map.

Demonstration of the corresponding receptors in the same cells suggests para- or autocrine mechanisms of action.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms local cutaneous expression of POMC, ACTH, alpha-MSH, beta-endorphin, and their corresponding receptors.

units.text: Afamelanotide is an MC1R agonist. In two sponsor-funded phase 3 RCTs in erythropoietic protoporphyria it increased pain-free time in direct sunlight (US trial, n=94: median 69.4 vs 40.8 hours over six months; EU trial, n=74: 6.0 vs 0.8 hours over nine months, with fewer phototoxic reactions). Both guides grade it A for EPP. Use outside EPP remains investigational (for example a phase 3 vitiligo trial started in 2023 with no results posted).

assertions.text: Afamelanotide is an MC1R agonist.
assertions.quote: Afamelanotide (Scenesse, Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals) is a potent analogue of human α-melanocyte–stimulating hormone (α-MSH). It is a tridecapeptide that binds to the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) in dermal cells, including melanocytes, and increases the production of eumelanin in the epidermis without the ultraviolet light–induced cellular damage that occurs when melanin production is stimulated by ultraviolet radiation.
assertions.note: Supported by the Langendonk et al. trial description.

assertions.text: In two sponsor-funded phase 3 RCTs in erythropoietic protoporphyria, afamelanotide increased pain-free time in direct sunlight (US trial, n=94: median 69.4 vs 40.8 hours over six months; EU trial, n=74: 6.0 vs 0.8 hours over nine months, with fewer phototoxic reactions).

In the European Union study, the duration of pain-free time after 9 months was also longer in the afamelanotide group than in the placebo group (median, 6.0 hours vs. 0.8 hours; P = 0.005), and the number of phototoxic reactions was lower in the the afamelanotide group (77 vs. 146, P = 0.04).

units.text: Melanotan II is a non-selective melanocortin agonist (MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, MC5R) that crosses into the brain. Its only controlled human data are a 1996 single-blind pilot in three men (tanning in two; nausea, yawning, spontaneous erections, somnolence) and a 1998 crossover in ten men with psychogenic erectile dysfunction; no trial has tested cosmetic tanning. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it C and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide D ('harms > benefit'); the course grades cosmetic use D.

assertions.text: Melanotan II is a non-selective melanocortin agonist (MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, MC5R) that crosses into the brain.
assertions.quote: Because melanotan II can cross the blood–brain barrier and is nonselective, it also activates the other MCRs, resulting in adverse events including fatigue, loss of appetite and penile erection.
assertions.note: Bohm et al. describe Melanotan II as a nonselective melanocortin receptor agonist that crosses the blood-brain barrier.

assertions.text: In a 1996 single-blind pilot trial in three men, Melanotan II produced tanning in two subjects along with nausea, yawning, spontaneous erections, and somnolence.
assertions.quote: Mild nausea, not requiring antiemetic treatment, was reported at most MT-II dose levels. A stretching and yawning complex appeared to correlate with the onset of spontaneous, penile erections which were intermittently experienced for 1-5 hours after MT-II dosing, depending on the MT-II dose.
assertions.note: Dorr et al. report the 1996 single-blind pilot in three men showing increased pigmentation in two subjects along with nausea, yawning, spontaneous erections, and somnolence.

assertions.text: A 1998 placebo-controlled crossover study evaluated Melanotan II in ten men with psychogenic erectile dysfunction.
assertions.quote: Ten men with erectile dysfunction of no known organic cause were entered in a double-blind, placebo controlled crossover study in which the erectogenic properties of Melanotan-II and a vehicle placebo were compared using real-time RigiScan monitoring.
assertions.note: Wessells et al. describe a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in ten men with psychogenic erectile dysfunction.

assertions.text: The Peptide Pocket Guide grades Melanotan II C and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades it D ('harms > benefit').
assertions.note: The cited guides are unavailable in the source text.

units.text: Reported harms of Melanotan II come from case reports and reviews: darkening and growth of existing naevi, eruptive and atypical (dysplastic) naevi, melanonychia; at least five melanomas reported during or after use, each in a person with other risk factors, so causation is unproven; ischaemic priapism needing surgery; sympathomimetic toxicity with rhabdomyolysis and renal dysfunction; FDA also lists posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome among published serious events.

assertions.text: Reported harms of Melanotan II include darkening and growth of existing naevi, as well as eruptive and atypical (dysplastic) naevi.
assertions.quote: In addition to these general risks, increasing numbers of case reports indicate that the unregulated use of both melanotan I and II is associated with cutaneous complications, particularly melanocytic changes in existing moles and newly emerging (dysplastic) nevi.
assertions.note: Habbema et al. confirm reports of melanocytic changes in existing moles and newly emerging dysplastic nevi with Melanotan II use.

assertions.text: Melanonychia has been reported as a harm of Melanotan II use.
assertions.note: The cited reference for melanonychia is unavailable and none of the other provided sources mention melanonychia.

assertions.text: At least five melanomas have been reported during or after Melanotan II use, each in a person with other risk factors, leaving causation unproven.
assertions.quote: There have been at least five reports of melanomas during or after melanotan II use. All individuals had other risk factors such as fair skin, excess sun exposure/tanning bed use and/or family history of melanoma.
assertions.note: Böhm et al. state that at least five melanomas have been reported and that all individuals had other risk factors.

assertions.text: Melanotan II has been reported to cause ischaemic priapism requiring surgical management.
assertions.quote: We describe in this case report a patient presenting with acute ischemic priapism after subcutaneous injection of melanotan II. The patient was initially managed with cavernosal aspiration and irrigation, and intracavernous injection of phenylephrine without achieving detumescence. After failing initial management, the patient underwent operative management with penoscrotal decompression, a promising alternative technique for the management of refractory ischemic priapism.
assertions.note: Mallory et al. report a case of acute ischemic priapism after Melanotan II injection requiring penoscrotal decompression surgery.

assertions.text: Melanotan II has resulted in sympathomimetic toxicity with rhabdomyolysis and renal dysfunction.
assertions.quote: Melanotan II use resulted in systemic toxicity including apparent sympathomimetic symptoms, rhabdomyolysis, and renal dysfunction.
assertions.note: Nelson et al. conclude that Melanotan II resulted in sympathomimetic symptoms, rhabdomyolysis, and renal dysfunction.

assertions.text: The FDA lists posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome among published serious adverse events associated with Melanotan II.
assertions.quote: Published case reports discuss serious adverse events including melanoma, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, sympathomimetic toxidrome and priapism.
assertions.note: The FDA Category 2 safety table lists posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome among published serious adverse events for Melanotan II.

units.text: Melanotan II sold online is of uncertain content: vials from three online shops held 43–88% of the labelled amount, with up to 5.9% unknown impurities, and TGA testing of five identically labelled seized nasal sprays found content varying more than twofold between bottles.

assertions.quote: Vials from two shops contained unknown impurities ranging from 4.1 to 5.9%; impurities from one shop were below the quantification limit. The total amount of melanotan II in vials ranged between 4.32 and 8.84 mg, although each shop claimed that vials contained 10 mg melanotan II.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms vials claimed to contain 10 mg actually contained 4.32 to 8.84 mg (43–88%) and unknown impurities ranged from 4.1 to 5.9%.

assertions.text: TGA testing of five identically labelled seized nasal sprays found melanotan II content varying more than twofold between bottles.
assertions.note: The cited TGA safety advisory source text is unavailable.

units.text: Melanotan II is approved for no therapeutic indication. US: FDA's compounding safety page (current as of 22 April 2026) lists it among nominations withdrawn from Category 2, citing impurity and immunogenicity risks and published reports of melanoma, PRES, sympathomimetic toxidrome and priapism. UK: MHRA (FOI 24/274, 17 April 2024) classes injectable products as medicines, says unauthorised medicines may not be sold, supplied or advertised, and advises users to stop immediately. Australia: TGA (17 August 2026) — prescription-only medicine, not approved as a tanning agent, no product on the ARTG.

assertions.text: Melanotan II is approved for no therapeutic indication.

assertions.note: The review states that Melanotan II is not approved for use in any therapeutic indication.

It is important to note that the sale, supply and advertising of unauthorised medicines is not permitted under the Human Medicines Regulations.

units.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats a personal or family history of melanoma as an absolute contraindication to Melanotan II. A case report describes crops of new atypical naevi and growth of existing naevi in a man with prior melanoma who self-injected an α-MSH analogue, with lightening after he stopped; MC1R activation does not prevent melanoma, and regular skin examination remains critical in high-risk people.

He developed crops of new pigmented nevi, many of which had atypical clinical and histopathologic features. The preexisting nevi became darker and acquired growth features. After alpha-MSH use was discontinued, the nevi progressively lightened and lost their growth features.

units.text: Skin monitoring matters with melanocortin agonists: during Melanotan II use, sequential videodermoscopy documented naevus changes that made naevus and melanoma hard to tell apart, and even the approved MC1R agonist's US label recommends a full-body skin examination twice yearly.

units.text: PTD-DBM fuses a cell-penetrating TAT fragment to a sequence that competes CXXC5 off Dishevelled, activating Wnt/β-catenin; in mice it accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced follicle neogenesis, and CXXC5 is raised in human balding scalp. This single 2017 study from the developer's group is its whole evidence: no human trial is published (PubMed) or registered (ClinicalTrials.gov) as of 24 September 2026. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it D.

units.text: Thymulin is a nine-residue thymic peptide that is biologically active only when zinc-bound. units.text: Growth hormone acts mainly in the dermis: its receptor is expressed more by dermal fibroblasts than keratinocytes, and GH increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis. IGF-1, made locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, acts on keratinocytes through the IGF-1 receptor; in culture IGF-1, not GH, drives keratinocyte proliferation.

assertions.text: Growth hormone activity is primarily evident in the dermis, where it supports collagen synthesis.
assertions.quote: GH activity, sometimes mediated via IGF-I, is primarily evident in the dermis, particularly affecting collagen synthesis.
assertions.note: The review explicitly notes that GH activity is primarily evident in the dermis, particularly affecting collagen synthesis.

assertions.text: Growth hormone receptor is expressed at higher levels in dermal fibroblasts than in keratinocytes, and GH increases fibroblast numbers.
assertions.quote: Northern analysis, using the cloned GH-R as probe, revealed relatively higher levels of GH-R transcripts in cultured human dermal fibroblasts compared to cultured keratinocytes or keratome biopsies.

assertions.note: IGF-1 transcripts were detected in fibroblasts and melanocytes but not keratinocytes, while IGF-1 receptor mRNA was abundant in keratinocytes.

units.text: GH secretion and IGF-1 decline progressively with age (the somatopause); IGF-1 must be read against age- and sex-adjusted ranges, so a value low for a young adult is often normal for age.

units.text: Human skin reflects the axis at its extremes: adults with GH deficiency have a thinner epidermis and reduced sweating on biopsy, not fully reversed by treatment of childhood-onset deficiency; in acromegaly, dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema thicken and puff the skin of the face, hands and feet.

units.text: In people with burns over 40% of body surface, recombinant GH shortened burn-wound and donor-site healing in pooled small randomized trials (13 RCTs, 701 people), with more hyperglycaemia; the evidence carries risk of bias.

units.text: In the US (21 U.S.C. 333(e), current text read September 2026), knowingly distributing human growth hormone for any use other than treating a disease or recognized condition authorised by FDA, on a physician's order, is a federal offence.

units.text: Tesamorelin, a GHRH analogue, reduced visceral fat by about 15% versus placebo at 26 weeks in two developer-run phase 3 RCTs (806 patients pooled), with subcutaneous fat unchanged; in the US it has been FDA-approved since 2010 for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy, and its label excludes weight loss. Both guides grade it A — for that indication only.

Skin puffiness due to dermal glycosaminoglycan accumulation and edema are most prominent in the face, hands and feet. units.text: Observed human data on IGF-1 and cancer are associations: higher circulating IGF-1 is linked with modestly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal and thyroid cancer, with reverse causation not excluded; acromegaly shows a slightly raised cancer incidence in pooled studies (SIR 1.5) that a nationwide cohort did not confirm (SIR 1.1).

assertions.text: Higher circulating IGF-1 is associated with higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal, and thyroid cancer.
assertions.quote: Higher IGF-I concentration was associated with increased risks of thyroid cancer [HR per 5 nmol/L higher concentration 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.01-1.37] in addition to colorectal (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.03-1.13), breast (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.07-1.15), and prostate cancer (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.05-1.12), and reduced risks of ovarian and liver cancer.
assertions.note: UK Biobank prospective analyses showed higher IGF-1 concentrations were associated with increased risks of thyroid, colorectal, breast, and prostate cancer.

assertions.text: Reverse causation cannot be excluded in observational findings relating IGF-1 to cancer risk.
assertions.quote: Mean follow-up was 6.9 years and the possibility that the observed associations may be influenced by reverse causality bias cannot be excluded.
assertions.note: The prospective study notes that reverse causality bias cannot be excluded.

assertions.text: Acromegaly shows a slightly raised overall cancer incidence in pooled studies (SIR 1.5).
assertions.quote: The meta-analysis yielded an SIR of overall cancer of 1.5 (95% CI, 1.2 to 1.8).
assertions.note: The meta-analysis of 23 studies found a standardized incidence ratio (SIR) of 1.5 for overall cancer in acromegaly.

assertions.text: A nationwide cohort study did not confirm an increased cancer incidence in acromegaly, reporting an SIR of 1.1.
assertions.quote: The cohort study identified 81 cases of cancer after exclusion of cases diagnosed within the first year [SIR 1.1; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.9 to 1.4].
assertions.note: The nationwide cohort study identified an SIR of 1.1 (95% CI 0.9-1.4).

units.text: GH treatment cohorts are largely reassuring for replacement: no clear raised cancer risk in 23,984 GH-treated children with growth failure and no other major disease, and a 2022 consensus found no association between GH replacement and primary tumour or recurrence; people with GH-receptor deficiency have very little cancer. No long-term cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for ageing or skin — the mitogenic risk there is plausible and unmeasured.

assertions.text: In a SAGhE cohort of 23,984 recombinant GH-treated children, there was no clear raised cancer risk among those with growth failure and no other major disease.
assertions.note: The cohort analysis of 23,984 GH-treated patients found no clear raised cancer risk in individuals with isolated growth failure without other major disease.

units.text: GRADE rates certainty in four levels (high, moderate, low, very low) for an outcome across a body of evidence, not for a single study or a molecule; randomized trials start high and observational studies start low.

assertions.text: GRADE specifies four levels of certainty/quality (high, moderate, low, very low) applied to a body of evidence rather than individual studies.
assertions.quote: GRADE specifies four categories-high, moderate, low, and very low-that are applied to a body of evidence, not to individual studies.
assertions.note: Balshem et al. explicitly state that GRADE specifies four categories (high, moderate, low, very low) applied to a body of evidence rather than individual studies.

assertions.text: Under GRADE, randomized trials begin as high-quality/certainty evidence and observational studies begin as low quality/certainty.
assertions.quote: Randomized trials begin as high-quality evidence, observational studies as low quality.
assertions.note: Balshem et al. state that randomized trials begin as high-quality evidence and observational studies as low quality.

units.text: Certainty is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency (unexplained variability across studies), indirectness (study PICO differs from the question), imprecision (confidence interval crossing the important-difference threshold) and suspected publication bias — which a body of small, industry-funded studies should raise — and can be rated up for large effects.

assertions.text: In GRADE, certainty of evidence is rated down for inconsistency, defined as unexplained variability in results across studies.
assertions.quote: This third article in a seven part series presents the Core GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach to deciding whether to rate down certainty of evidence due to inconsistency—that is, unexplained variability in results across studies.
assertions.note: Core GRADE defines inconsistency as unexplained variability across studies and rates down certainty accordingly.

assertions.text: Certainty of evidence is rated down for indirectness when study PICO differs substantially from the target question.
assertions.quote: When target and study PICOs differ substantially, studies provide indirect evidence and Core GRADE users may rate down the certainty of evidence as a result of this indirectness.
assertions.note: Core GRADE rates down certainty for indirectness when study PICOs differ substantially from the target PICO.

assertions.text: Certainty of evidence is rated down for imprecision when the confidence interval crosses the minimal/important difference threshold.
assertions.quote: Users then rate down for imprecision if the 95% confidence interval crosses the MID for benefit or harm.
assertions.note: Users rate down for imprecision when the confidence interval crosses the MID threshold.

assertions.text: A body of small, industry-funded studies should raise suspicion of publication bias.
assertions.quote: For publication bias, a body of evidence comprising small studies funded by industry should raise suspicion.
assertions.note: The guideline indicates that small industry-funded studies should raise suspicion of publication bias.

assertions.text: Certainty of evidence can be rated up for large effects.
assertions.quote: Core GRADE users appraising results from well conducted NSRI can consider rating up certainty of evidence when risk ratios from pooled estimates suggest large or very large effects.
assertions.note: Core GRADE allows rating up certainty when pooled estimates suggest large or very large effects.
