units.text: A Cochrane methodology review of 75 papers found industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; moderate-quality evidence) and favourable conclusions (RR 1.34) than non-industry studies, a bias not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessment.

assertions.text: A Cochrane methodology review found industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; moderate-quality evidence) and favourable conclusions (RR 1.34) than non-industry studies.
assertions.quote: Industry sponsored studies more often had favorable efficacy results, RR: 1.27 (95% CI: 1.17 to 1.37) (25 papers) (moderate quality evidence), similar harms results RR: 1.37 (95% CI: 0.64 to 2.93) (four papers) (very low quality evidence) and more often favorable conclusions RR: 1.34 (95% CI: 1.19 to 1.51) (29 papers) (low quality evidence) compared with non-industry sponsored studies.
assertions.note: The Cochrane review findings match the reported risk ratios and certainty ratings.

assertions.text: The industry bias in research outcomes is not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessment.
assertions.quote: Our analyses suggest the existence of an industry bias that cannot be explained by standard 'Risk of bias' assessments.
assertions.note: The review authors conclude that industry bias cannot be explained by standard risk of bias assessments.

units.text: Both Hormonaly guides attach an A–D letter to the evidence for a specific use — adapted from GRADE's four levels — which rates evidence, not legality; mechanistic appeal never raises a grade, and grade and regulatory status are separate checks to clear.

units.text: In the US, 503A compounding by a licensed pharmacist or physician for an identified patient is exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and cGMP only if the bulk substance meets a USP/NF monograph, or failing that is a component of an approved drug, or failing that is on the 503A bulks list — and is made by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis. The statute sets no purity figure.

assertions.text: In the US, 503A compounding by a licensed pharmacist or physician for an identified patient is exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and cGMP only if the bulk substance meets a USP/NF monograph, or failing that is a component of an approved drug, or failing that is on the 503A bulks list.
assertions.quote: State-licensed physicians and pharmacists that compound under section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) may only compound drug products using bulk drug substances that: Comply with an applicable United States Pharmacopeia (USP) or National Formulary (NF) monograph if one exists, and the USP chapter on pharmacy compounding; Are components of FDA-approved drug products
assertions.note: 21 U.S.C. § 353a and FDA guidance confirm that exemptions apply when bulk substances meet a USP/NF monograph, are components of approved drugs, or appear on the 503A bulks list.

assertions.text: The bulk substance must be made by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis.
assertions.quote: In addition, bulk drug substances must be accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis and must have been manufactured by an establishment registered with FDA under section 510 of the FD&C Act.
assertions.note: FDA explicitly states bulk drug substances must have been manufactured by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis.

assertions.text: The statute sets no purity figure.
assertions.quote: (A) compounds the drug product using bulk drug substances, as defined in regulations of the Secretary published at section 207.3(a)(4) of title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations— (i) that— (I) comply with the standards of an applicable United States Pharmacopoeia or National Formulary monograph, if a monograph exists, and the United States Pharmacopoeia chapter on pharmacy compounding ;
assertions.note: Section 353a specifies compliance standards (monographs, approved drug components, or bulk list) without specifying an explicit numerical purity figure.

units.text: 503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with FDA, must meet cGMP, are inspected on a risk-based schedule, report adverse events and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions; their products are exempt from approval and adequate-directions requirements, so they remain unapproved.

assertions.text: 503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with the FDA, must comply with cGMP, are inspected according to a risk-based schedule, and report adverse events.
assertions.quote:
Outsourcing facilities:

must comply with CGMP requirements;

are inspected by FDA according to a risk-based schedule; and

must meet certain other conditions, such as reporting adverse events and providing FDA with certain information about the products they compound.
assertions.note: The FDA guidance page confirms that 503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with FDA, must comply with CGMP, are inspected on a risk-based schedule, and report adverse events.

assertions.text: 503B outsourcing facilities may compound drugs without obtaining patient-specific prescriptions.
assertions.quote: An outsourcing facility may or may not obtain prescriptions for identified individual patients.
assertions.note: The statute explicitly states that an outsourcing facility may or may not obtain prescriptions for individual patients.

assertions.text: Drugs compounded by an outsourcing facility are exempt from FDA approval and adequate directions for use requirements.
assertions.quote: Drugs compounded by an outsourcing facility can qualify for exemptions from FDA approval requirements and the requirement to label products with adequate directions for use, but not from current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) requirements.
assertions.note: The FDA source confirms that compounded drugs from outsourcing facilities qualify for exemptions from FDA approval and adequate directions for use requirements.

units.text: As of 22 September 2026 the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) holds six substances, none a peptide, unchanged since 2019; listing carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.

assertions.quote: A final regulation was issued in February 2019, List of Bulk Drug Substances That Can Be Used To Compound Drug Products in Accordance with Section 503A of the FD&C Act , in which FDA placed six substances on the list, identified and did not place four other substances on the list, and established the criteria to evaluate substances for inclusion on the list.

assertions.text: None of the substances on the 503A bulks list is a peptide.
assertions.note: The provided text does not identify the specific substances on the list or mention whether any is a peptide.

assertions.text: Listing on the 503A bulks list carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.
assertions.note: The provided text does not discuss FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy for listed substances.

units.text: Categories 1–3 are FDA's interim enforcement posture while nominations are evaluated, not listing. As of 14 May 2026 Category 1 includes GHK-Cu except injectable routes and 503A Category 2 holds six substances; BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, injectable GHK-Cu, LL-37 and melanotan II sit in a table of withdrawn nominations whose safety concerns remain posted.

assertions.text: Categories 1–3 represent the FDA's interim enforcement posture while bulk drug substance nominations are evaluated rather than final listing.
assertions.quote: The agency issued this interim policy to avoid unnecessary disruption to patient treatment while FDA evaluates the bulk drug substances nominated for inclusion on the 503A bulks list . The interim policy describes three categories of bulk drug substances nominated for use in compounding.
assertions.note: The FDA explains that categories 1–3 are part of an interim enforcement policy while nominated substances are evaluated for the 503A bulks list.

assertions.text: As of 14 May 2026, Category 1 includes GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration).
assertions.quote: GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) will be added back to category 1.
assertions.note: The FDA Category 1 list updated May 14, 2026 explicitly includes GHK-Cu except for injectable routes of administration.

assertions.quote: Advisory committees make non-binding recommendations to the FDA, which generally follows the recommendations but is not legally bound to do so.
assertions.note: The advisory committee webpage confirms that committee recommendations are non-binding advice.

assertions.text: FDA's review staff concluded the evaluation criteria weigh against placing BPC-157 on the 503A Bulks List.

assertions.note: FDA staff concluded that the criteria weigh against adding BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate to the 503A Bulks List.

units.text: Since 23 March 2020 FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, chemically synthesized or not, so such products are biological products; tesamorelin and hyaluronidase were deemed biologics licences on that date, and biologics are not eligible for the 503A or 503B compounding exemptions.

assertions.text: Since 23 March 2020 FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, chemically synthesized or not, making such products biological products.
assertions.note: The provided source texts mention removing the chemically synthesized polypeptide exclusion, but do not contain the specific definition of a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin and hyaluronidase applications were deemed biologics licenses on 23 March 2020.
assertions.quote: FDA has provided below a list of each approved application for a biological product under the FD&C Act that was deemed to be a license (i.e., an approved biologics license application (BLA)) for the biological product on March 23, 2020.
assertions.note: The FDA list confirms both hyaluronidase and tesamorelin acetate NDAs were deemed to be BLAs on March 23, 2020.

assertions.text: Biological products subject to licensure are not eligible for the section 503A or 503B compounding exemptions.
assertions.quote: This transition affects compounding under sections 503A and 503B of the FD&C Act because, beginning on March 23, these transitioning biological products will not be eligible for the exemptions for compounded drugs under sections 503A and 503B of the FD&C Act.

units.text: How residues are counted can decide classification: a federal district court in 2025 upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide (39-alpha-amino-acid backbone plus a two-residue side chain) is not a protein, remanding only the 'analogous to a protein' question; the appeal was pending as of the latest filings found (June 2026).

assertions.text: A federal district court in 2025 upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide (comprising a 39-alpha-amino-acid backbone plus a two-residue side chain) is not a protein, remanding only the 'analogous to a protein' question to the agency.
assertions.quote: The Motion is granted on the claim that FDA's justifications for failing to designate retatrutide as an "analogous product" were arbitrary and capricious. The Motion is denied on the claim that FDA's refusal to designate retatrutide as a protein, and hence as a biological product, violates the agency's own regulations.
assertions.note: The district court order confirms retatrutide's structure, grants summary judgment to FDA on the protein definition, and vacates/remands on the analogous-to-a-protein determination.

assertions.text: The appeal of the district court decision was pending as of June 2026.
assertions.note: The appellate docket source is unavailable, so the pending status cannot be verified from the provided text.

units.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's attestation for a named lot — mass spectrometry for identity (observed against expected mass), HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results. It cannot establish that the vial in hand is that lot, how it was stored since testing, or that the product is sterile and suitable to inject; lot-less, chromatogram-less, stale (over 12 months) and endotoxin-less certificates are warning signs.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's attestation for a named lot covering identity (e.g., mass spectrometry), purity (e.g., HPLC), endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal, and solvent results.
assertions.note: The provided available source texts do not define the standard contents of a certificate of analysis in this manner, and the cited handbook is unavailable.

recheck.note: The provided source texts do not contain this definition or complete list of testing attributes for a certificate of analysis.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis cannot establish that the vial in hand belongs to the tested lot, how it was stored since testing, or that the product is sterile and suitable to inject.
assertions.note: The provided available source texts do not address these specific limitations of a certificate of analysis.

recheck.note: The provided text does not discuss the specific limitations of a Certificate of Analysis regarding physical lot matching, post-testing storage history, or finished product sterility and suitability for injection.

units.text: There is no single universal endotoxin limit per milligram: FDA's guidance says the limit is calculated with the USP method from the product's dosage regimen and strength, and some routes (intrathecal, ophthalmic) differ.

assertions.text: FDA guidance states that endotoxin limits must be calculated using USP methods from the product's dosage regimen and strength rather than relying on a universal fixed limit table.
assertions.quote: The endotoxins limit table is out of date due to the increase in numbers of dosage (regimes) and drug strengths since the publication of the 1987 Guidance.  The appropriate way to establish the endotoxins limit is to use the calculation methods provided in the USP or AAMI standards.
assertions.note: FDA guidance notes that fixed limit tables are outdated and limits should be calculated using USP or AAMI standards based on dosage regimens and strengths.

assertions.text: Endotoxin limits for certain administration routes, including intrathecal and ophthalmic routes, differ from the standard calculations for parenteral products.
assertions.quote: Intrathecally-administered products, ophthalmics, or devices (see question 11 for devices) may have endotoxins limits that are not based on the calculation for parenterally administered products.
assertions.note: FDA guidance explicitly states that intrathecal products and ophthalmics may have limits not based on the parenteral calculation.

assertions.quote: Due to inconsistencies in the nomination packages, the nominated BDS is unclear from both nominators of BPC-157-related BDSs. For example, the nominated BDS is not consistent with what is listed in the Certificate of Analysis (CoA).
assertions.note: The FDA briefing notes that although BPC-157 free base was indicated by the UNII codes/nominations, the CoAs provided were for BPC-157 acetate.

assertions.text: Publicly available BPC-157 certificates mostly report purity alone without impurity limits.
assertions.quote: We conducted literature searches and found that most CoAs for BPC-157 (free base) only contain purity testing results, an example of which is shown below (Figure 2). There is no information about the impurity limits/testing results in the CoA to demonstrate control of the impurity profile of BPC- 157 (free base).
assertions.note: The briefing notes that literature searches revealed most publicly available CoAs contain purity testing alone without impurity limits.

assertions.text: The CoA provided by the nominator did not mention an endotoxin test.

units.text: Paperwork and contents can diverge: three semaglutide vials bought from illegal online pharmacies measured 7.7–14.4% purity against 99% on the label, 29–39% more peptide than labelled and endotoxin in every vial; a seized injection vial held an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue identifiable only by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Neither study concerns skin peptides.

assertions.text: Three semaglutide vials bought from illegal online pharmacies measured 7.7–14.4% purity against 99% on the label.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, the measured semaglutide purity was significantly low, ranging between 7.7% and 14.37% and deviating from the 99% claimed on product labels by manufacturers.
assertions.note: The study found measured purity of the three delivered semaglutide vials ranged from 7.7% to 14.37% despite 99% claimed on labels.

assertions.text: The purchased semaglutide vials contained 29–39% more peptide than labelled.
assertions.quote: The semaglutide content of samples substantially exceeded labeled amounts by 28.56%-38.69%, although no peptide-like impurities were identified.
assertions.note: The semaglutide content exceeded labeled amounts by 28.56% to 38.69%.

assertions.text: Endotoxin was detected in every purchased semaglutide vial.
assertions.quote: The lyophilized peptide samples were devoid of viable microorganisms at the time of testing; however, endotoxin was detected in all samples with levels ranging between 2.1645 EU/mg and 8.9511 EU/mg.
assertions.note: Bacterial endotoxin was confirmed in all three delivered vial samples.

assertions.text: A seized injection vial held an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue identifiable only by high-resolution mass spectrometry.
assertions.quote: Therefore, in the present work, a qualitative analysis by liquid chromatography coupled to high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry with a quadrupole time-of-flight analyzer was performed to identify a new heptapeptide (MW = 874.02 Da) - a glycine analogue of GHRP-2.
assertions.note: The study identified a novel glycine analogue of GHRP-2 in a seized vial using high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry, but does not state it is the only method capable of identification.

units.text: In the US the regime follows intended use and route: appearance claims make a cosmetic (no premarket approval), while a claim to affect structure or function — such as 'regenerate cells' — makes a drug, and 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning; dietary supplements are not approved before sale, their makers being responsible for safety and labelling.

assertions.text: In the US, cosmetic classification is based on intended use (altering appearance) and cosmetics do not require premarket approval.
assertions.quote: Under the FD&C Act, cosmetic products and ingredients, with the exception of color additives, do not require FDA approval before they go on the market.
assertions.note: The FDA explains that cosmetics intended to alter appearance do not require FDA approval before marketing.

assertions.text: A claim to affect structure or function—such as 'regenerate cells'—makes a product a drug under US regulation.
assertions.quote: Such claims establish the product as a drug because the intended use is to treat or prevent disease or otherwise affect the structure or functions of the human body. Some examples are claims that products will restore hair growth, reduce cellulite, treat varicose veins, increase or decrease the production of melanin (pigment) in the skin, or regenerate cells.
assertions.note: The FDA explicitly gives cell regeneration as an example of a claim establishing a product as a drug.

assertions.text: The term 'cosmeceutical' has no legal or statutory meaning under US law.
assertions.quote: The FD&C Act does not recognize any such category as "cosmeceuticals." A product can be a drug, a cosmetic, or a combination of both, but the term "cosmeceutical" has no meaning under the law.
assertions.note: The FD&C Act does not recognize the category and the term has no meaning under the law.

assertions.text: Dietary supplements are not approved prior to sale in the US, with manufacturers responsible for product safety and labeling.
assertions.quote: That means that these firms are responsible for evaluating the safety and labeling of their products before marketing to ensure that they meet all the requirements of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as amended by DSHEA and FDA regulations.
assertions.note: Under DSHEA, manufacturers are responsible for safety and labeling prior to marketing rather than obtaining premarket approval.

units.text: 'Off-label' describes unapproved use of an approved drug; a never-approved peptide has no label to depart from, introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act, and FDA has warned a compounding pharmacy that its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products did not qualify for the 503A exemptions.

assertions.quote: Unapproved use of an approved drug is often called “off-label” use.
assertions.note: FDA explicitly defines off-label use as the unapproved use of an approved drug.

units.text:
The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages · three lessons
Lesson 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ · Lesson 1.2 Receptor maps and what they prove · Lesson 1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis.
Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 01
The skin makes its own hormones.
This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.
1.2 Receptor maps: what a cell atlas can and cannot show
Set your path
How will you use this course?
The evidence, grades and regulatory facts are the same for everyone. What changes, in every module, is the 'what you do …

assertions.text: The skin produces its own hormones and responds to circulating hormones from the blood.
assertions.quote: In the widest sense, the human skin and its cells are the targets as well as the producers of hormones.
assertions.note: The cited review confirms that human skin acts as both a target for circulating hormones and a producer of hormones.

units.text:
Lesson 1.1 · Concept
Four units, one circuit.
Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.
Four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal
Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream
Mechanism register: cell, tissue and animal work
Narration: Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts…
units.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

assertions.text: Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ compartmentalized into four regulatory units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal.
assertions.quote: This skin neuro–immuno–endocrine system is compartmentalized through the formation of epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal regulatory units.
assertions.note: Slominski 2025 explicitly defines the skin neuro-immuno-endocrine system as comprising epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal units.

assertions.text: Skin cells across these units can produce hormones/neuroendocrine factors and participate in immune responses.
assertions.quote: Immunocompetent skin-resident cells ( Supplementary Table 1 ) and circulating immune cells have the capability to produce neuroendocrine factors and express corresponding receptors 25 , 35 .
assertions.note: The source notes that skin-resident and circulating cells possess immune competence and the capability to synthesize neuroendocrine factors.

assertions.text: Skin units communicate locally between neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and via release of mediators into the bloodstream.
assertions.quote: These immuno–endocrine units communicate among themselves through soluble factors released by skin cells or circulating immune cells or through rapid transmission by directly or indirectly activated sensory nerves in a bidirectional manner, allowing efficient communication among different compartments.
assertions.note: The review documents communication via local soluble mediators, direct sensory nerve activation, and systemic circulation.

units.text:
Mechanism
A steroid factory with local axes.
Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Each row names the evidence it rests on, because most of it comes from cells, tissue kept alive outside the body, or mice.
Steroid synthesis
Cholesterol to cortisol, androgens and estrogens
CYP11A1 starts the chain; 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase and aromatase activate precursors from the blood. Cell and tissue studies.
HPA-like loop
CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with feedback
Human scalp follicles kept alive in culture. Ex vivo, human tissue.
Keratinocyte glucocorticoids
Set local immune tone
Genetic deletion in mouse keratinocytes. Animal evidence.
Thyroid-like loop
TRH, TSH and deiodinases → T3
Keratinocyte growth and the hair cycle. Mostly mouse models.
Somatotropic loop
GH and …
units.sourceNote: Slominski 2013 · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Mancino 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6

assertions.text: Skin cells contain enzymes to synthesize steroids from cholesterol (starting with CYP11A1) or activate systemic precursors via enzymes like 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, and aromatase.
assertions.quote: Most recently it has been established that skin cells contain the entire biochemical apparatus necessary for production of glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens either from precursors of systemic origin or, alternatively, through the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone and its subsequent transformation to biologically active steroids.

assertions.text: Human scalp hair follicles in organ culture operate an HPA-like loop where CRH drives POMC/ACTH and cortisol synthesis with negative feedback.

units.text:
Local or systemic
Three directions of traffic.
Hormone signals in skin run in three directions. Some are made and used in the same patch of skin. Some arrive from the blood. A few leave the skin and act on the rest of the body. Knowing which one you are looking at decides whether the answer lies in the skin or in a systemic assessment.
Local loop
Made and used in the skin
Between neighbouring cells, back on the same cell, or inside it
Body to skin
A circulating hormone acting on skin
The skin finding can be the visible sign of a systemic disorder
Skin to body
A skin product entering the circulation
The skin acting as an endocrine gland for other organs
Callout: Before you treat a skin finding, decide which direction it runs.

units.text:
What changes in practice
Read the skin before the serum.
The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.
A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment
Narration: Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the who…

units.text:
Lesson 1.2 · Concept
A map of fourteen million cells.
The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers
Narration: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such …

units.text:
What the atlas is
Prediction, in the authors' own words.
The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.
379
hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell
Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · about 14 million cells and nuclei · 47 human tissues
What it means: The atlas shows which skin cells carry the RNA to make or sense a hormone. That is a well-founded hypothesis about where to look.
What it does not mean: It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.

What changes in practice
A map to confirm, then a trial.
Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.
A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin

A brochure for a hormone-containing serum cites a single-cell atlas showing that dermal fibroblasts carry the RNA for that hormone's receptor. What does that finding establish?
Explanation: A receptor on the map is where the question starts.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That the serum reaches those fibroblasts and improves the skin.
Explanation: That needs penetration data and a clinical trial; an RNA map provides neither.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That skin secretes the hormone and needs it replaced when levels fall.
Explanation: The finding concerns a receptor, and RNA says nothing about secretion or deficiency.
Correct answer: That fibroblasts may respond to the hormone: a hypothesis to confirm at the protein, function and clinical level.
Explanation: Correct. The atlas's authors call such predictions putative and hypothesis-generating.

units.text:
Lesson 1.3 · Concept
Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.
A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.
Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age
Narration: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as inte…
units.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ressler 2006 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Haykal 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

assertions.text: Senescent cells enter permanent cell-cycle arrest while remaining metabolically active and secreting inflammatory cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes, and growth factors (the SASP).

assertions.note: Haykal et al. describe senescent cells as permanently arrested yet metabolically active entities secreting the SASP.

assertions.text: The SASP was characterised in cultured human cells following DNA damage / genotoxic stress.
assertions.quote: We show that human cells induced to senesce by genotoxic stress secrete myriad factors associated with inflammation and malignancy. This senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) developed slowly over several days and only after DNA damage of sufficient magnitude to induce senescence.
assertions.note: Coppé et al. characterised the SASP in cultured human cells following genotoxic stress/DNA damage.

assertions.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a increase with donor age in both the epidermis and the dermis.
assertions.quote: We show that the number of p16INK4A positive cells is significantly higher in elderly individuals compared to the younger age groups. The number of p16INK4A positive cells was found to be increased in both epidermis and dermis, compartments with strictly different proliferative activities.
assertions.note: Ressler et al. showed p16INK4a-positive cells increase significantly with age in both human epidermal and dermal compartments.

assertions.note: Haykal et al. note that keratinocytes, fibroblasts, and melanocytes in skin can all undergo senescence.

assertions.text: No single universal marker unequivocally identifies a senescent cell.
assertions.quote: However, a significant hurdle in the aging field has been the identification of a universal biomarker that facilitates the unequivocal detection and quantification of senescent cell types in vitro and in vivo .
assertions.note: Wang & Dreesen highlight the ongoing difficulty in finding a single universal biomarker for unequivocal senescent cell detection.

Human evidence
Three years of perceived age.
In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.
3 years
younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age
Waaijer et al., 2016 — 178 adults aged 45–81, Leiden Longevity Study, sun-protected arm biopsies
What it means: Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.
What it does not mean: It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.

units.text:
Four registers
Human, mouse or dish?
Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.
Mechanism
A collagen-fragmentation loop
Skin collagen falls with age. Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen; in culture, fragmentation raises MMP-1 further. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible, not shown.
Human evidence
Association
p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age
Animal evidence
Causation, in mice
Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice; skin was not the endpoint
Open question
Do senotherapies change human skin?
Small pilots measuring tissue markers; no randomized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2…

assertions.text: Skin collagen falls with age.
assertions.quote: Skin collagen decreased with age and was less in the females at all ages.
assertions.note: Shuster 1975 confirms that skin collagen decreases with advancing age.

assertions.text: Aged human dermis shows increased fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen, and culturing fibroblasts in fragmented collagen increases MMP-1 further.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, fibroblasts cultured in fragmented collagen lattices express elevated levels of MMP-1, AP-1, and alpha2beta1 integrin. Importantly, culture in fragmented collagen raises intracellular oxidant levels and treatment with antioxidant MitoQ(10) significantly reduces MMP-1 expression. units.text:
Where the evidence is strongest
The levers with trials behind them.
Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.
Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)
Topical retinoids for photoageing: GRADE A
Senolytics for skin: no clinical-outcome trials yet

Systemic hormones and the skin · three lessons
Lesson 2.1 Cortisol on the skin · Lesson 2.2 Estrogen, menopause and collagen · Lesson 2.3 Skin signs that need an endocrinologist.
Module 02 · Hormones written on the skin
The face that might be a diagnosis.
Most skin changes you see are ageing or lifestyle. A few are the first visible sign of endocrine disease. In three lessons you will separate them: what local and systemic hormones do to skin, what hormone therapy can and cannot do for it, and which signs belong with an endocrinologist.
2.1 Cortisol on the skin: local 11β-HSD1 and Cushing's syndrome
2.2 Estrogen, menopause and collagen: what the trials show
Your turn
'Is this cortisol face?'
One question to close lesson 2.1.
'Hormones for my skin.'
One question to close lesson 2.2.
Hair removal, or referral?
One question to close lesson 2.3.
Cortisol signatures: local 11β-HSD1 and Cushin…

Mechanism
The skin regenerates its own cortisol.
Skin expresses the machinery of a local stress axis, including CRH and POMC with its product ACTH. Keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts also carry 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples its activity is higher with age and in sun-exposed skin, and local cortisol availability is set independently of blood levels. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice lacking the enzyme kept their dermal thickness with age.
Local axis: CRH, POMC and ACTH are made in skin
11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol inside skin cells
Mechanism register: human samples, cultured cells and mice
Narration: Picture the skin as a small endocrine organ with its own stress axis. Skin cells make CRH and ACTH, the same signals that drive the adrenal glands, and they carry the rece…

units.text:
The evidence
Rare, and usually from a prescription.
Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon: European population studies put it at two to three new cases per million people a year. The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, from glucocorticoids given as medicine. The Endocrine Society therefore asks for a drug history first, covering tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-bleaching products, and recommends testing when features are multiple and progressive.
2–3
new cases of endogenous Cushing's syndrome per million people per year (European population studies)
As cited in the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, 2008
What it means: A round, puffy face in an aesthetic clinic is almost always something other than Cushing's syndrome, and when cortisol excess is real it most often comes from a glucocorticoid the patient is already using.

units.text:
What changes in practice
Reassure the many, refer the few.
When a patient asks about 'cortisol face', start with the drug history: steroid creams, skin-lighteners, herbal tonics and injections. Then look for the discriminating features. Without them, the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society recommends against widespread testing. With them, especially when they are progressing, the next step is formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a consumer cortisol panel answers the wrong question.

assertions.quote: After excluding exogenous glucocorticoid use, we recommend testing for Cushing's syndrome in patients with multiple and progressive features compatible with the syndrome, particularly those with a high discriminatory value, and patients with adrenal incidentaloma.
assertions.note: The abstract explicitly states this recommendation.

units.text:
Lesson 2.2 · Concept
Estrogen and the dermis.
Skin carries estrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ and the membrane receptor GPER) in both sun-protected and sun-damaged sites. In postmenopausal women, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in sun-protected hip skin; photoaged facial skin showed no such response. After menopause, small biopsy studies found skin collagen and thickness falling year by year, following years since menopause more closely than age. That is mechanism and natural history. What hormone therapy does to a face is a separate question.
Receptors: ERα, ERβ and GPER in aged and photoaged skin
Topical estradiol raises collagen in sun-protected skin only
Collagen loss follows years since menopause
Narration: Estrogen is the hormone the guide says dominates the visible ageing of women's skin, so start with what it does in the dermis. Skin carries estrogen receptors…
units.sourceNote: Rittié 2008 · Thornton 2013 · Brincat 1985 · Affinito 1999 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 9

assertions.text: Skin carries estrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ, and GPER) in both sun-protected and sun-damaged sites.
assertions.quote: Surprisingly, no significant changes in production were observed in women or men after 2-week estradiol treatment of photoaged forearm or face skin, despite similar expression of estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30) in aged and photoaged skin.
assertions.note: Rittié et al. confirm similar expression of ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30 in aged and photoaged skin.

assertions.text: Two weeks of topical estradiol increased collagen production in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women, whereas photoaged facial or forearm skin showed no response.
assertions.quote: Two-week topical estradiol treatment stimulates collagen production in sun-protected hip skin, but not in photoaged forearm or face skin, in postmenopausal women and aged-matched men.
assertions.note: Rittié et al. found topical estradiol stimulated collagen in sun-protected hip skin but not photoaged forearm or face skin.

assertions.text: Postmenopausal decline in skin collagen and skin thickness correlates more closely with years of estrogen deficiency/menopause than with chronological age.
assertions.quote: This decrease in skin thickness and collagen content in elderly females correlates with the period of estrogen deficiency rather than chronological age.
assertions.note: Thornton reports that decreases in skin thickness and collagen correlate with the duration of estrogen deficiency rather than chronological age.

units.text:
The evidence
One to two per cent a year.
In small biopsy studies of postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness fell by about 1–2% a year, in step with bone mass, and followed years since menopause more than age. Reviews, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide, quote a steeper early loss of up to 30% in the first five years. That figure traces to the same small studies, and a check of their abstracts in September 2026 did not find it stated.
fall in skin collagen content and thickness per year after menopause (small biopsy studies)
Brincat et al., 1987 — in parallel with bone mass
What it means: Estrogen withdrawal is a measurable contributor to dermal thinning, and it follows the menopause clock rather than age alone.
What it does not mean: It does not show that hormone therapy restores a younger-looking face. These are small observational studies, mostl…
units.sourceNote: Brincat 1985, 1987 · Affinito 1999 · Thornton 2013

assertions.text: In postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness decline by about 1–2% per year in step with bone mass, correlating with years since menopause rather than age alone.
assertions.quote: The skin collagen content, skin thickness, metacarpal index, and forearm bone mineral content in postmenopausal women showed a similar decline of between 1-2% per year after the menopause.
assertions.note: Brincat et al. (1987) reported a 1–2% per year postmenopausal decline across skin collagen, thickness, and bone mass correlated with years since menopause.

assertions.text: Reviews cite an early skin collagen decrease of up to 30% in the first five years following menopause.
assertions.quote: Type I and III skin collagen is thought to decrease by as much as 30% in the first five years after menopause, 27 , 28 which parallels the reduction in bone mass observed in post-menopausal women.
assertions.note: Thornton (2013) reviews literature stating skin collagen decreases by as much as 30% in the initial five postmenopausal years.

units.text:
Human evidence
Biopsy gains, mirror results.
Hormone therapy has two kinds of trial behind it. Small trials measure the dermis; larger trials measure the face. They point in different directions, so read them separately. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the North American Menopause Society rates the same evidence 'limited or inconsistent'. This course grades the structural gains C and teaches the negative wrinkle trials alongside them.
Systemic HT · skin thickness and collagen
Increased · GRADE C
Two small RCTs (60 and 41 women) measured hip and upper-arm skin
Systemic HT · facial wrinkles
No difference · GRADE B
485 women for 48 weeks on low-dose therapy; a four-year trial in recently menopausal women also found no difference
Pooled analysis (2023)
Positive, heterogeneous · GRADE C
Small studies, some non-randomized, varying widely; its authors…
units.sourceNote: Maheux 1994 · Sauerbronn 2000 · Phillips 2008 · Owen 2016 · Pivazyan 2023 · Creidi 1994 · Ashcroft 1999 · NAMS 2022

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the North American Menopause Society rates the same evidence 'limited or inconsistent'.
assertions.note: The provided NAMS 2022 abstract does not discuss skin ratings or rate evidence as 'limited or inconsistent', and the guide is unavailable.

assertions.text: Two small RCTs (60 and 41 women) measured hip and upper-arm skin for changes in skin thickness and collagen from systemic HT.
assertions.quote: Forty-one postmenopausal women were randomly allocated to receive either hormonal replacement (valerate estradiol--2 mg/day for 21 days and cyproterone acetate--1 mg/day for 10 days) or placebo, both in a cyclic scheme for 6 months. Neither patients nor investigators were aware of the group allocation. Histologic changes were evaluated by skin biopsy of the left upper arm at baseline and after 6 months of treatment, utilizing computerized image analysis to assess the ratio area of epidermis/basement membrane length (AE/BML), ratio area of keratin/basement membrane length (AK/BML) and collagen and elastic fibers content.
assertions.note: Maheux 1994 evaluated 60 women at the great trochanter (hip) and Sauerbronn 2000 evaluated 41 women via upper-arm skin biopsy.

assertions.text: A 48-week RCT of 485 women on low-dose therapy and a four-year trial in recently menopausal women found no difference in facial wrinkles with systemic HT.
assertions.quote: Four hundred eighty-five subjects were enrolled in this 48-week randomized, double-blind study.
assertions.note: Phillips 2008 and Owen 2016 both reported no significant improvement in facial wrinkling scores.

assertions.text: A 2023 pooled analysis included small and non-randomized studies with high heterogeneity, and its authors do not propose hormone therapy as an independent skin treatment.
assertions.quote: While not claiming that MHT can or should ever be considered as an independent treatment for skin ageing, we still believe that our results are interesting as they indicate a beneficial effect of MHT on the skin, despite studies showing a negative effect of MHT on other organs.
assertions.note: Pivazyan 2023 noted heterogeneity and explicitly stated they do not claim MHT can or should be considered an independent treatment for skin ageing.

assertions.text: A 24-week RCT of topical estrogen on the face found improvements in skin thickness and fine lines, while a biopsy study found no collagen response in photoaged facial skin.
assertions.quote: In conclusion, Premarin cream produced better results than the placebo cream; the difference was statistically significant for skin thickness and fine wrinkles.
assertions.note: Creidi 1994 found significant gains in thickness and fine wrinkles at 24 weeks, whereas Rittié 2008 showed no collagen production increase in photoaged face skin.

assertions.text: A small randomized study in healthy older adults showed topical estrogen accelerated acute wound healing.
assertions.quote: Eighteen health status-defined females (mean age, 74.4 years) and eighteen males (mean age, 70.7 years) were randomized in a double-blind study to either active estrogen patch or identical placebo patch attached for 24 hours to the upper inner arm, through which two 4-mm punch biopsies were made.
assertions.note: Ashcroft 1999 showed accelerated acute wound healing from topical estrogen in 36 healthy elderly participants.

units.text:
Regulatory status and indications
Symptoms and bone. Skin is a bystander.
In the US, as of February 2026, FDA-approved menopausal hormone therapy is for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss. FDA's 2025–26 labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning; skin did not become an indication. The North American Menopause Society's 2022 statement finds benefit outweighs risk for bothersome symptoms and bone protection when therapy starts before 60 or within 10 years of menopause, and finds insufficient evidence for compounded 'bioidentical' hormones. Under US rules an over-the-counter 'hormone cream' is an unapproved drug. For the skin itself, daily sunscreen has a large randomized trial behind it, and one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for fine facial wrinkl…
units.sourceNote: FDA, 10 Nov 2025 and 12 Feb 2026 · 21 CFR 310.530 · NAMS 2022, 2020 · Manson 2013 · Hughes 2013 · Renova label

assertions.text: In the US, as of February 2026, FDA-approved menopausal hormone therapy is for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss.
assertions.quote: The FDA has approved multiple hormone therapies for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal dryness and discomfort, and preventing bone loss.
assertions.note: FDA documents confirm approved indications for menopausal hormone therapy include moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal symptoms, and prevention of bone loss.

assertions.note: The FDA approved the removal of cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and probable dementia statements from the boxed warning.

Intervention Random assignment into 4 groups: daily use of broad-spectrum sunscreen and 30 mg of β-carotene, daily use of sunscreen and placebo, discretionary use of sunscreen and 30 mg of β-carotene, and discretionary use of sunscreen and placebo.

units.text:
A 52-year-old with no hot flashes, no sleep disturbance and no vaginal symptoms asks for estrogen 'to stop my face ageing'. What does the evidence support?
Explanation: Symptoms decide hormone therapy; skin gets skin-directed care.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Estrogen rebuilds collagen, so hormone therapy is a reasonable anti-ageing choice.
Explanation: That is the mechanism talking. Small trials show thicker skin, the largest trials found no difference in wrinkles, and skin is not an approved indication.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): A compounded 'bioidentical' estrogen face cream avoids the risks of systemic therapy.
Explanation: Compounded 'bioidentical' preparations lack efficacy and safety data and carry quality concerns; the menopause society says preference alone should not justify them.
Correct answer: Skin alone is not a reason to start hormone …

assertions.text: The largest trials of hormone therapy for facial aging found no statistically significant difference in wrinkles compared to placebo.
assertions.quote: There were slight decreases in all parameters for all treatment groups for the primary subject end points, but there were no statistically significant differences between the NA/EE groups and placebo.
assertions.note: Phillips et al. found no statistically significant differences in facial wrinkling between continuous combined hormone therapy and placebo.

assertions.text: Skin aging is not an FDA-approved indication for menopausal hormone therapy.
assertions.quote: The FDA has approved multiple hormone therapies for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal dryness and discomfort, and preventing bone loss.
assertions.note: The FDA lists approved hormone therapy indications as hot flashes, vaginal dryness/discomfort, and bone loss prevention, with no indication for skin aging.

assertions.note: The provided abstract of the NAMS 2022 position statement does not mention compounded bioidentical hormone therapy.

assertions.text: Daily sunscreen has a large randomized controlled trial supporting its efficacy in retarding skin aging.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: A randomized trial of 903 adults demonstrated that daily sunscreen reduced skin aging by 24% over 4.5 years compared to discretionary use.

units.text:
Lesson 2.3 · Concept
Some syndromes show on the skin first.
A handful of inherited endocrine syndromes appear on the skin before the glands declare themselves. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), multiple facial angiofibromas and collagenomas are common. In Carney complex, lentigines on the lips, eyelids and canthi, blue naevi and small skin myxomas sit alongside myxomas of the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN2A, an itchy, rippled, pigmented plaque between the shoulder blades can precede medullary thyroid cancer.
MEN1: facial angiofibromas, collagenomas
Carney complex: lip and eyelid lentigines, myxomas
MEN2A: lichen amyloidosis between the shoulder blades
Narration: Some endocrine syndromes are written on the skin years before the glands give them away. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type one, most patients in one careful series had several facial angiofi…
units.sourceNote: Darling 1997 · Kirschner 2000 · Correa 2015 · Stanescu 2024 · Lause 2017 · the guide's inherited-syndromes chapter

assertions.text: In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), facial angiofibromas and collagenomas are common cutaneous manifestations, identical to lesions seen in tuberous sclerosis.
assertions.quote: Multiple facial angiofibromas were observed in 28 (88%) of the patients with MEN1, with 16 patients (50%) having 5 or more. Angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those in individuals with tuberous sclerosis. Collagenomas were observed in 23 patients (72%).
assertions.note: Darling et al. found facial angiofibromas in 88% and collagenomas in 72% of patients with MEN1, noting angiofibromas were identical to those in tuberous sclerosis.

assertions.text: Carney complex is commonly caused by inactivating mutations in the PRKAR1A gene.
assertions.quote: The disease is caused by inactivating mutations or large deletions of the PRKAR1A gene located at 17q22–24 coding for the regulatory subunit type I alpha of protein kinase A (PKA) gene.
assertions.note: Correa et al. confirm that Carney complex is caused by inactivating variants in the PRKAR1A gene in over 70% of patients.

assertions.text: Carney complex features lentigines on the lips, eyelids, and canthi, blue nevi, skin and cardiac myxomas, and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease.
assertions.quote: The most common endocrine tumor in CNC is primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD), a cause of (ACTH)-independent overproduction of cortisol .
assertions.note: Correa et al. describe spotty pigmentation on lips, eyelids, and canthi, cutaneous and cardiac myxomas, blue nevi, and PPNAD-induced cortisol overproduction.

assertions.text: In MEN2A, cutaneous lichen amyloidosis—a pruritic, pigmented plaque in the interscapular/scapular area—can precede the presentation of medullary thyroid cancer.
assertions.quote: Typically, CLA is detected at an early age (from childhood until young adulthood) before the actual MTC identification unless RET screening protocols are already applied.
assertions.note: Stanescu et al. report that cutaneous lichen amyloidosis predominantly affects the scapular area and typically appears before medullary thyroid cancer is diagnosed.

units.text:
The evidence
Eighty-eight per cent.
In a consecutive series of 32 people with MEN1 examined at the US National Institutes of Health, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas. The angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those of tuberous sclerosis. The authors concluded that angiofibromas in someone without tuberous sclerosis call for biochemical testing for MEN1.
of 32 people with MEN1 had multiple facial angiofibromas
Darling et al., 1997 — collagenomas in 72%
What it means: Multiple facial angiofibromas are common in MEN1 and can be its first visible sign; in someone without tuberous sclerosis they are a reason for endocrine testing, whatever the cosmetic plan.
What it does not mean: It does not mean a single facial papule is MEN1. This is one small referral-centre series, and angiofibromas have other causes, tuberous sclerosis above all.

assertions.note: The abstract confirms that in a consecutive sample of 32 patients with MEN1 at the National Institutes of Health, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas.

assertions.text: The angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those of tuberous sclerosis.

assertions.note: The study confirms that the angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those seen in tuberous sclerosis.

assertions.note: The authors state that observing angiofibromas in patients without tuberous sclerosis necessitates biochemical testing for MEN1.

units.text:
Concept
The everyday endocrine signs.
Most endocrine skin signs you meet come from common disease. New generalised darkening, strongest in skin creases, scars, mucosa and sun-exposed skin, can signal primary adrenal insufficiency, which can turn into a life-threatening crisis. Hirsutism that appears fast, keeps progressing, or comes with a deepening voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely. Velvety dark plaques of acanthosis nigricans track insulin resistance, pretibial myxoedema points to Graves' disease, and cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.
Darkening in creases, scars and gums: adrenal insufficiency
Rapid hirsutism or virilization: exclude a tumour
Acanthosis, pretibial plaques, dry cool skin: metabolic and thyroid
Narration: Most of the endocrine skin signs you will actually meet come from common conditions. New, generalised darkening, most obvious …
units.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guidelines: Bornstein 2016, Martin 2018 · Lause 2017 · the guide's ch. 5 referral list

assertions.text: The Endocrine Society recommends diagnostic testing for primary adrenal insufficiency in patients with indicative symptoms or signs, with a low diagnostic and therapeutic threshold in acutely ill patients.
assertions.quote: We recommend diagnostic tests for the exclusion of primary adrenal insufficiency in all patients with indicative clinical symptoms or signs. In particular, we suggest a low diagnostic (and therapeutic) threshold in acutely ill patients, as well as in patients with predisposing factors.
assertions.note: The Endocrine Society guideline explicitly recommends diagnostic testing for primary adrenal insufficiency in symptomatic patients and suggests a low threshold in acutely ill individuals.

assertions.text: Pretibial myxoedema is a physical sign associated with Graves' disease.
assertions.quote: Physical signs in a patient with Graves’ disease often include sweating, tremor, a diffuse goiter, weight loss, digital clubbing, pretibial myxedema, and numerous cardiovascular changes, including tachycardia, arrhythmias, and bounding peripheral pulses ( 33 ).
assertions.note: Pretibial myxedema is listed among the characteristic physical signs of Graves' disease.

assertions.text: Rapidly progressing hirsutism, deepening voice, or clitoromegaly suggests an androgen-secreting tumour, and more than half of those tumours are malignant.
assertions.note: The provided abstract of the Endocrine Society hirsutism guideline does not mention rapid progression, virilization signs, or malignancy rates of androgen-secreting tumours.

assertions.text: Velvety dark plaques of acanthosis nigricans track insulin resistance.
assertions.note: Acanthosis nigricans and its association with insulin resistance are not mentioned in the provided text.

assertions.note: The association of cold, dry, or coarse skin with hypothyroidism is not described in any of the provided source texts.

Triage
Where does this skin finding go?
Seven presentations from an aesthetic list, and three routes. Your job is to route the finding, not to make the diagnosis. The verdict and the source behind each appear as you answer.
Urgent assessment
Before any cosmetic treatment
Findings that suggest a hormone-secreting tumour or an adrenal crisis
Endocrine referral
Planned work-up

No endocrine flag on this alone
Skin-directed care
Common findings without discriminating features; reassess if others appear

Fictional case
Freckles before the wedding.
A 29-year-old asks for laser removal of 'freckles' on her lips and at the corners of her eyes before her wedding. You notice a soft, skin-coloured papule on one eyelid. She mentions her father had 'a heart tumour' removed in his thirties. This is a fictional case built from the lesson's evidence; choose the first move that fits it.
Lip and canthal lentigines: typical of Carney complex
Eyelid papule: a possible cutaneous myxoma
A family heart tumour: the reason not to wait

While you examine her you notice a soft, skin-coloured bump on one eyelid. She mentions that her father had a heart tumour removed in his thirties. Pigmented spots at the corners of the eyes…

assertions.text: Pigmented spots at the inner or outer corners of the eyes (canthal lentigines) are seen in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.
assertions.quote: inner or outer canthal pigmentation such as the one shown here is only seen in CNC and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome making it diagnostic for these two conditions.
assertions.note: Correa et al. (2015) state that inner or outer canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.

assertions.text: Cutaneous myxomas in Carney complex commonly favour sites including the eyelids and ears.
assertions.quote: Cutaneous myxomas (Figure 1D–F) are found in 30–55% of CNC patients and usually appear in the eyelid, external ear canal, breast nipples, and the genitalia .
assertions.note: Correa et al. (2015) state that cutaneous myxomas usually appear in the eyelid, external ear canal, breast nipples, and genitalia.

units.text:
What do you do first?
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Proceed with the laser: lentigines are benign and she has a deadline.
Explanation: The spots may well be benign. Their distribution, the eyelid papule and the family history are what matter, and together they flag a possible syndrome.
Correct answer: Pause the cosmetic plan, document the findings and family history, and refer her promptly for endocrine and genetic assessment.
Explanation: Right. Canthal and lip lentigines with a possible myxoma and a family cardiac tumour fit Carney complex, where early echocardiographic screening matters. You route; the specialist diagnoses.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Order a cortisol test to check for Cushing's before deciding.
Explanation: Cortisol excess is one feature of Carney complex, but a single test neither assesses the syndrome nor its cardiac risk. Referral…

assertions.text: Canthal and lip lentigines, myxomas, and cardiac tumours are characteristic clinical features that fit a diagnosis of Carney complex.
assertions.quote: Spotty skin pigmentation with typical distribution (lips, conjunctiva and inner or outer canthi, vaginal and penile mucosal)Myxoma** (cutaneous and mucosal) or cardiac myxoma**
assertions.note: Corney complex diagnostic criteria include typical spotty pigmentation (lips, canthi) and myxomas.

assertions.text: Early detection and regular screening with echocardiography are essential in Carney complex due to the risks of cardiac myxomas.
assertions.quote: Myxomas can completely occlude a valvular orifice and may cause sudden death . This is why early detection and regular screening with echocardiography are essential ; cardiac CT or MRI may also be used for the detection of these tumors, especially in post-operative hearts with altered anatomy .
assertions.note: The source emphasizes that regular echocardiographic screening is essential to detect cardiac myxomas early.

assertions.text: Cortisol excess is a feature of Carney complex.
assertions.quote: The most common endocrine tumor in CNC is primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD), a cause of (ACTH)-independent overproduction of cortisol .
assertions.note: The review notes that PPNAD causes overproduction of cortisol in patients with Carney complex.

Matrix peptides and wound healing · three lessons
Lesson 4.1 Copper peptides · Lesson 4.2 Signal peptides, oral collagen and SNAP-25 mimics · Lesson 4.3 Repair peptides and the compounding line.
Module 04 · Matrix peptides and wound healing
The peptide your patient already bought.
Most skin peptides reach your clinic before any evidence does. In three lessons you will sort them by what the human trials actually show, who paid for those trials, and where each one stands with the regulator.
4.1 Copper peptides: GHK and GHK-Cu
4.2 Signal peptides, oral collagen and the 'topical Botox' family
4.3 Repair peptides, one negative trial, and the compounding line
Set your path
How will you use this module?
The evidence, grades and regulatory status are the same for everyone. What changes is the 'what you do next' at the end of each lesson, so it fits what your licence lets you do.
Choose the one c…

Mechanism
A plasma tripeptide with a copper habit.
GHK is a tripeptide found in human plasma, first described in 1973. Bound to copper it becomes GHK-Cu, which is proposed to deliver copper to enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and lysyl oxidase and to switch on wound-healing and antioxidant gene programmes. Most of that mechanistic literature comes from the group that discovered the peptide.
Endogenous: GHK circulates in human plasma
Proposed: copper delivery to matrix and antioxidant enzymes
Mechanism register only — written largely by the originator
Narration: Start with the molecule. GHK is a three-amino-acid peptide that circulates in human plasma; it was first described in 1973. It binds copper readily, and the copper complex, GHK-Cu, is what skin-care labels mean when they say copper peptide. The proposed mechanism is that GHK-Cu delivers copper to enzymes that build and protect…
units.sourceNote: Pickart & Thaler 1973 · Pickart 2008, 2015, 2018 · Peptide Pocket Guide

assertions.text: GHK is a tripeptide naturally present in human plasma that was first described in 1973.
assertions.quote: The human copper-binding peptide GHK-Cu (glycyl- l -histidyl- l -lysine) is a small, naturally occurring tri-peptide present in human plasma that also can be released from tissues in case of an injury. Since its discovery in 1973, GHK-Cu established itself as a powerful protective and regenerative ingredient, which is currently widely used in skin and hair products [ 1 ].
assertions.note: Supported by the review, which confirms GHK is a naturally occurring tripeptide in human plasma discovered in 1973.

assertions.text: GHK readily binds copper ions to form the complex GHK-Cu.
assertions.quote: Subsequent studies established this activity as a tripeptide with an amino acid sequence glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine with a strong affinity for copper that readily formed the complex GHK-Cu.
assertions.note: Supported by text describing GHK's strong affinity for copper and formation of GHK-Cu.

assertions.text: GHK-Cu is proposed to deliver copper to enzymes involved in matrix formation and antioxidant defense, and to modulate gene expression involved in tissue repair.
assertions.quote: The most distinctive feature of GHK is its ability to form complexes with copper (II) [ 51 ]. This is very important since copper is required for more than a dozen vital enzymes in the human body and skin including those that participate in connective tissue formation, antioxidant defense, and cellular respiration.
assertions.note: Supported by discussion of GHK-Cu delivering copper to cuproenzymes involved in connective tissue and antioxidant defense, and modulating gene expression.

units.text:
Human evidence
One indexed randomized trial.
A search of PubMed in September 2026 found one randomized controlled trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin: 2006, healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing. The cosmetic trials cited for anti-ageing claims are manufacturer-sponsored and not indexed. Both Hormonaly guides grade topical use C. A phase 2 trial of a topical GHK-Cu wound gel has been recruiting since 2026.
1
indexed randomized trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin
Miller et al., 2006 — healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing, not photoageing
What it means: The human evidence for topical GHK-Cu is small: one small indexed trial plus sponsor-run cosmetic studies. GRADE C is the honest ceiling.
What it does not mean: It does not show that GHK-Cu fails, that it treats photoageing, or anything about injecting it. A thin evidence base is an unknown, not a negative.

Four registers
Keep the four answers apart.
Every peptide question has four separate answers. For GHK-Cu they point in different directions, which is exactly why they must not be blended into one sentence.
Mechanism
Plausible
Copper delivery to matrix and antioxidant enzymes; gene-expression data from the originator
Human evidence
Topical: GRADE C · Injectable: none
One small indexed RCT and sponsor-run cosmetic trials; no randomized trials of injection
Regulatory status (US, 14 May 2026)
Non-injectable: 503A Category 1
Category 1 means FDA is still evaluating and does not intend to act against compounders who meet its conditions; an advisory-committee consultation is planned before the end of February 2027. The injectable route has no such standing.

Does it reach the dermis?
Penetration data are in vitro and depend on how they are measured

What changes in practice
Serum yes, syringe no.
Topical GHK-Cu is a reasonable cosmetic conversation at GRADE C. Injected GHK-Cu is a different product: no randomized trials, injection-site pain and rash are common because copper irritates tissue, and in the US the injectable route sits outside the Category 1 listing.
Topical: modest, small-trial support
Injectable: anecdote, common local reactions
Say which route you mean every time

Injected GHK-Cu is not the same product in a stronger form. units.text:
Lesson 4.2 · Concept
Three families, one question: who ran the trial?
Signal peptides such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (pal-KTTKS, Matrixyl) are meant to tell fibroblasts to make matrix. SNAP-25 mimics — Argireline, its longer cousin SNAP-8, and Leuphasyl — are meant to quieten expression lines. Oral collagen peptides are swallowed, not applied. All three families have a trial record, and in all three the question that matters most is who funded it.
Signal peptides: 'make more matrix'
SNAP-25 mimics: 'relax the line'
Oral collagen: the supplement aisle
Narration: Lesson two covers three families that fill the cosmetic and supplement shelves. Signal peptides, like palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, sold as Matrixyl, are fragments of matrix proteins meant to tell fibroblasts to make more collagen. SNAP-25 mimics, Argireline and its longer cousin SNAP-8, copy part of a nerve-terminal protein that bo…

The evidence
Twenty-three trials, split by who paid.
Pooled, oral collagen trials show better hydration, elasticity and wrinkle scores, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades them C. A 2025 meta-analysis split the same kind of trials by funding and by quality. The benefit appeared only in pharmaceutical-funded and low-quality trials. Unfunded and high-quality trials showed no effect.

What it does not mean: It does not show collagen is harmful, and it does not rule out benefit for an individual. It is a statement about the evidence, and it says nothi…

units.text:
What changes in practice
Cosmetic, supplement, drug: three rulebooks.
In the US, cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs, and their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework. Oral collagen is a dietary supplement: it may not claim to treat disease, and product quality and content vary. Neither route has to prove efficacy before sale — which is why the funding question matters.
Cosmetic ingredient: no efficacy approval needed
Dietary supplement: no disease claims; quality varies
Say 'modest, small-trial' — never 'topical Botox'
Narration: Now the regulatory register, stated for the United States. Cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs; their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework, and nobody has to prove they work before they are sold. Oral collagen is sold as a dietary supplement, so it cannot claim to treat a disease, and what is in the tub vari…

Lesson 4.3 · Concept
Rodents, a fragment, and a tripeptide.
BPC-157 rests on a large rodent literature, mostly from one research group, and on uncontrolled human case series. TB-500 is not thymosin β4: it is a seven-residue fragment of it, identified by analysing the product itself, and no trial has tested the fragment. KPV, a tripeptide from the end of α-MSH, calms inflammation in mouse colitis and has no randomized human trial.
BPC-157: rodents and case series
TB-500: a fragment, never trialled
KPV: mouse colitis only

units.text:
The evidence
Zero published efficacy trials.
As of September 2026 no randomized efficacy trial of BPC-157 in people has been published. What exists on ClinicalTrials.gov: a 2015 phase 1 safety study that never posted results, a completed 2025 single-arm product study with no results posted, a phase 2 randomized trial recruiting since 2026, and a phase 1 trial planned for 2027.
published randomized efficacy trials of BPC-157 in people (September 2026)
Registered: phase 1 (2015, no results) · single-arm product study (2025, no results) · phase 2 RCT (recruiting) · phase 1 RCT (planned 2027)
What it means: Whether BPC-157 helps people heal is unknown. The enthusiasm rests on rodents and uncontrolled case series.
What it does not mean: It does not show BPC-157 is ineffective or unsafe. Absence of trials is absence of evidence, and this figure will change when the registered trials report.

units.text:
Worked example
Two trials, one peptide: LL-37.
LL-37, the skin's own cathelicidin, is the one repair peptide with two randomized trials in hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers. Read them in order.
First trial (2014)
Positive at low dose
First-in-human, randomized, dose-ranging; 34 patients
Second trial (2021)
Negative in the full cohort
Multicentre phase IIb, placebo-controlled; only a post hoc subgroup signal
Who ran them
The developer, both times
Sponsorship does not make a trial wrong; it is one more reason to wait for replication
Grade
C — inconsistent
A small positive trial followed by an adequately powered negative one
Callout: A small positive trial is a hypothesis. LL-37 is what happens when someone tests it.

units.text:
Follicle, pigment and melanocortins · three lessons
Lesson 5.1 The hair follicle as an endocrine mini-organ · Lesson 5.2 Afamelanotide, Melanotan II and the melanocortin receptors · Lesson 5.3 Investigational hair peptides, graded.
Module 05 · Follicle, pigment and melanocortins
A spray for the scalp, a tan in a vial.
Two requests reach aesthetic clinics well ahead of their evidence: a peptide to regrow hair and an injection to tan. In three lessons you will see how the follicle and the pigment system run on the skin's own hormones, why one melanocortin drug is approved while its gray-market cousin is approved nowhere, and how to grade the hair peptides patients bring to you.
Your turn
Shedding after the baby.
One question to close lesson 5.1.
'The approved one is the same thing.'
One question to close lesson 5.2.
'The new minoxidil'?
One question to close lesson 5.3.
Melanocortins: appr…

Mechanism
A follicle that runs its own hormones.
Human scalp hair follicles kept alive in the laboratory answer corticotropin-releasing hormone by making ACTH and α-MSH and secreting cortisol, with a feedback loop like the adrenal axis. They also run a growth hormone and IGF-1 loop of their own. Locally made dihydrotestosterone shrinks genetically susceptible scalp follicles, the process behind pattern hair loss. Growing follicles are shielded from immune attack, and alopecia areata begins when that shield fails.
Local stress axis: CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with feedback
Local androgen switch: testosterone → DHT in the scalp
Immune privilege: its collapse drives alopecia areata
Narration: Think of the hair follicle as a small gland. When researchers keep human scalp follicles alive in culture, the follicles answer corticotropin-releasing hormone the way the pituitary and adrenal glands do. …
